fields.analysis:
# Context and constraints for `session recap`

## Why now

E-1914's reworked `session list` made task-less sessions visible for the first
time (they used to carry a discussion summary; now the columns are the active
task's id and title, so they render blank). Seeing one immediately raises "what
was that session about, and is it worth resuming?" — and there is currently no
way to answer it.

E-1918 auto-creates a task titled `Auto-resumed task for session ES-NNN` on
resume precisely BECAUSE the user cannot name it. `session recap` is the
companion that lets them find out: additional to E-1918, not an alternative.
Expected to be reached for rarely — only when someone is triaging a task-less
session out of `session list`.

## HARD REQUIREMENT — do not re-open E-1470

Headless `claude -p` calls must scrub `TMUX_PANE` (or set the hook-skip marker)
before spawning. E-1470 recorded this exact failure:

> Headless `claude -p` calls run `subprocess.run` with no env scrub, inheriting
> the caller `TMUX_PANE`. The headless call gets a new session UUID and fires a
> hook → `TouchSession(new_uuid, inherited_pane)`; the collision UPDATE then sets
> `state=ended` on the CALLING live session (same pane, different uuid).

The observed damage was that `endless session id` and `endless task add` broke
until the next Stop hook, because the resolver filters `state != ended` and the
caller had just been marked ended by its own subprocess. **Recap was one of the
two callers that hit it.** Reintroducing a `claude -p` call without the scrub
reintroduces the bug.

## This does NOT re-open E-1906

E-1906 ("Remove the vestigial session-recap flag now that one session maps to one
task") removed an **automatic, background** recap flag, on the stated premise
that *"one session now maps to one task and `endless task report` covers the
handoff."*

A task-less session is exactly the case where that premise does not hold, so an
**on-demand, user-invoked** recap sits in the gap E-1906's reasoning leaves open
rather than contradicting it. The distinction to preserve: nothing may generate
recaps on its own schedule, for sessions nobody asked about.

E-1906 dropped the old recap columns via a change file, so caching needs a **new**
column with its own migration — not a resurrection of the dropped one.

## Shape

```
endless session recap <session-id|task-id>
```

- Accepts a session ref (`ES-NNN`, integer, UUID prefix) or a task id (`E-NNN`),
  resolving a task to its most-recent session. Take `ES-` from the start; E-1918
  is fixing the entry points that lack it, and a new command must not add another.
- Shells out to `claude -p` with haiku or sonnet over the session's transcript.
- Caches into the new `sessions` column so repeat calls are free.
- **Invalidates** — TTL, or cleared on the session's next turn — so a later call
  reflects the current transcript rather than a stale summary. A recap that
  silently describes a conversation as it was ten turns ago is worse than none.

## Open questions for planning

- Model choice: haiku (cheap, likely sufficient for "what was this about") vs
  sonnet. Possibly a flag.
- Invalidation mechanism: a TTL is simplest; clearing on the next recorded turn
  is more correct but needs a hook touchpoint.
- Behavior for an ended session whose transcript file is gone.

## Settled: `session list` may show a CACHED recap, never generate one

A task-less row in `session list` has nothing in its Task/Title columns, so it may
fall back to this session's recap — **but only if `session recap` has already
cached one.** The listing must never generate a recap on read: it renders up to
`--limit` rows, so a generate-on-read fallback would fan out into one `claude -p`
per blank row, which is precisely the automatic-background behavior E-1906 removed
and E-1470's env-scrub bug lived in.

So the rule is: read the cache if present, render blank if not, never fill it.

**Knock-on for E-1914's omit-by-default rule.** E-1914 omits task-less sessions
from `session list` until `--all`, on the grounds that they have nothing to show. A
cached recap gives such a row content, which partly undoes that premise. Decide at
planning time between:

  - leave the omission as-is, and surface cached recaps only under `--all`
    (simplest; the rows a user has bothered to recap are the ones they were
    already inspecting with `--all`), or
  - un-omit a task-less session *once it has a cached recap*, since it now has
    something to say (more useful, but makes row inclusion depend on cache state,
    which is a surprising thing for a listing to do).

The first is the safer default. Either way this must not silently re-establish the
Summary column E-1914 removed.

## From the description

shell out to 'claude -p' (haiku or sonnet) over the session transcript and print a recap, cached in a new sessions column with TTL-or-clear-on-next-turn invalidation so a later call reflects the current transcript. Hard requirement: the headless call must scrub TMUX_PANE or set the hook-skip marker, or it re-opens E-1470 (the headless call false-ended the CALLING session).

fields.title: Decide what task-keyed session rows do when an ID is reused
fields.description: Decide whether session, notice and next-task rows keyed on a task ID without a foreign key stay attached to that ID once the task is removed and its ID reused.
fields.notes: the same failure E-1915 fixed for task_deps.
fields.context: session_tasks, session_hidden_tasks, session_notices and project_next_tasks/_pending all key on a task id with no FK, by design ('the row must outlive its task'), and all resurrect against an unrelated task when the id is reused —
fields.analysis:
E-1915 guarded `task_deps` and `decision_relations`, the two tables whose rows
are *relations* and can therefore be cleared with an `unlink`. Four more tables
key on a task id with no foreign key, deliberately, and every one of them
resurrects on id reuse the same way `task_deps` did:

| Table                  | Rows survive a task delete because…                          | What a reused id inherits |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| `session_tasks`        | "rows must outlive their referenced session/task" (schema)    | A session is reported as having touched a task it never saw. `task show` renders this under "Touched by:". |
| `session_hidden_tasks` | "the row must be able to outlive its session or task"         | A brand-new task is silently invisible in one session's `session status`. Nothing indicates why. |
| `session_notices`      | "a notice must be able to outlive its session or task"        | An undelivered notice about a dead task is delivered as though it were about the new one. |
| `project_next_tasks` / `project_next_pending` | No FK to `tasks` at all (`task_id` is TEXT) | A curated "next" entry for a removed task reappears pointing at unrelated work. |

Measured, not inferred: after `endless task remove 8001` in an isolated DB,
`session_tasks` held 2 rows for 8001 (the executor adds a `revisited` touch on
the delete itself), `session_hidden_tasks` 1, `session_notices` 1,
`project_next_tasks` 1. For contrast, `task_landings` (FK ON DELETE CASCADE),
`sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id` (FK ON DELETE
SET NULL) all cleared correctly, and `session_task_relations` turned out to be
the relation-kind vocabulary table (goal/surfaced/revisited), not task-keyed at
all — so the two tables E-1915's plan named as suspects are both clean.

## Why this is not just "apply the E-1915 guard here"

E-1915's answer was *refuse the removal and make the operator unlink*. That
answer does not transfer. There is no `unlink` for "session 9001 touched task
8001" — it is history, not a relation, and the schema comments say outliving the
task is the POINT. So the guard would be unclearable: a task touched by any
session could never be removed.

The real question this task has to answer is one design call, shared by all
four: when a task id is freed, does a row that deliberately outlives its task
stay attached to that id?

Sketch of the options, not a decision:

- **Purge on delete.** Contradicts the stated intent of every one of the four
  schema comments; loses the "session N touched task M" audit record.
- **Tombstone the id.** Stop reusing task ids, or record freed ids, so nothing
  can inherit. Fixes the whole class at once, including anything added later,
  but is the largest change.
- **Qualify the rows.** Store enough alongside the task id (the task's created_at,
  or a generation counter) that a consumer can tell "this row is about the task
  that HELD id 8001", and filter on read.
- **Repair, don't prevent.** Extend E-1915's `reconcile` repair to these tables.
  Cheapest, and it inherits E-1915's ordering hazard: it can only clean orphans
  whose id is still free.

They may not all want the same answer — `session_tasks` is an audit record,
`session_hidden_tasks` is live display state, `project_next_tasks` is a curated
list. Filed as one task because the design call is shared; split if the answers
diverge.

Nothing here is implemented. E-1915's reconcile repair covers `task_deps` and
`decision_relations` only.

## From the description

E-1915's answer (refuse the removal, make the operator unlink) does not transfer: there is no unlink for a session touch.

Needs one design call, shared by all four: does a row that outlives its task stay attached to a freed id?

fields.title: Stop task import's bulk clear orphaning task relations
fields.description: Stop task import's replace and clear options leaving removed tasks' relation rows behind, deciding whether the refuse-and-unlink approach task remove uses suits a bulk refresh.
fields.context: Reproduced: after a re-import with --replace the imported task is gone and its task_deps row survives.
fields.analysis:
E-1915 put the relation guard in `remove_item` (`src/endless/task_cmd.py`), so
it only covers `endless task remove`. Two other commands delete `tasks` rows and
neither passes through it:

- `endless task import <file> --replace` → `_do_import` (`task_cmd.py` ~line 852)
- `endless task import-json --clear`     → `import_json` (`task_cmd.py` ~line 2240)

Both emit `task.bulk_cleared`, which `execTaskBulkCleared`
(`internal/events/executor.go` ~line 831) executes as
`DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id = ? AND source_file = ?` — no relation
cleanup, no guard.

Reproduced in an isolated DB:

    endless task import PLAN.md          # creates task 1 from PLAN.md
    endless task link 1 --to E-8500 --type blocks
    endless task import PLAN.md --replace

    tasks WHERE id=1     -> 0     (deleted)
    task_deps            -> 1     (orphaned, still says "1 blocks 8500")

Same failure mode as the original bug: invisible until id 1 is reused, then
wrong with the authority of a computed fact.

## The open question

Whether E-1915's answer — REFUSE and make the operator unlink — is right here is
not obvious, which is why this is filed rather than folded in. `task remove` is
a deliberate act on one named task, so a refusal costs one command. A re-import
is a bulk refresh over a whole file; refusing it because one imported task
picked up a relation could deadlock the workflow, and the operator may not even
know which relation the guard means.

Options, not a decision:

- Same guard, same refusal. Consistent, possibly obstructive.
- Refuse but list, with an explicit opt-out flag on the import.
- Delete the relations along with the tasks. Rejected for `task remove` on the
  grounds that a severed relation is unrecoverable — but an imported task's
  relations may be judged cheaper.
- Leave it to the repair. E-1915's `reconcile` repair already sweeps these
  orphans up on the next `project list` / `project scan`, and inherits its
  ordering hazard: it only helps while the freed id is still free.

Note the last option means this is *partially* mitigated today — the window is
"between the re-import and the next reconcile", not forever.

## From the description

Whether E-1915's refuse-and-unlink answer suits a bulk import refresh is the open question.

fields.description: Fix task remove --cascade to count descendants before deleting the subtree, so it reports the real number removed instead of always zero.
fields.context:
`endless task remove 8600 --cascade` on a parent with a child and a grandchild prints 'Removed E-8600 and 0 descendant(s)'.

Pre-existing; found while verifying E-1915's cascade guard.
fields.analysis:
`remove_item` in `src/endless/task_cmd.py` emits `task.deleted` and THEN counts
the descendants it is about to report:

    emit_event(kind="task.deleted", ...)     # the Go executor deletes the subtree here
    ...
    desc_count = db.scalar(
        "WITH RECURSIVE tree(id) AS ("
        "  SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE parent_id = ?"
        "  UNION ALL"
        "  SELECT t.id FROM tasks t JOIN tree ON t.parent_id = tree.id"
        ") SELECT count(*) FROM tree", (item_id,))

`emit_event` runs the executor synchronously, so by the time the query runs the
rows are already gone and the recursive CTE seeds from nothing. The count is
therefore always 0.

Reproduced in an isolated DB — a parent with a child and a grandchild:

    $ endless task remove 8600 --cascade
    • Removed E-8600 and 0 descendant(s): P

Two tasks were deleted alongside the root; the line says none were.

Pre-existing, not introduced by E-1915 — E-1915's guard raises before
`emit_event` and does not touch this path. Found while verifying the
`--cascade` behavior.

The fix is to capture `desc_count` BEFORE the emit, next to the existing
`child_count` read. E-1915 already computes exactly this id set before the emit
(`_removal_id_set(item_id, cascade)`), so the descendant count is
`len(_removal_id_set(item_id, True)) - 1` and no second query is needed.

## From the description

Fix is to count before the emit — E-1915's _removal_id_set() already computes that id set.

fields.title: Replace task deletion with a removed flag
fields.description: Replace hard deletion of tasks, sessions and decisions with a removed flag on the row so its ID is never reused, and make every read path filter out removed rows.
fields.notes: Absorbs E-1930 and E-1931.
fields.analysis:
Absorbs E-1930 (extend the policy to non-task entities) and E-1931 (drop pending
notices), both closed obsolete in favour of this task.

## Scope: which entities are covered

ED-1547 covers any id that something outside its own row refers to — logically,
not only where SQLite declares a FOREIGN KEY. That is tasks, sessions and
decisions. A junction or child table whose surrogate primary key nothing else
stores and nobody types stays an unrestricted hard delete.

## Three parts

**1. Convert each covered entity's delete path.** Set a new `removed` flag on the
row rather than issuing a DELETE. Sessions are the known live exposure:
`session_tasks.session_id` refers to a session with no declared constraint,
exactly as `task_id` does, and `task_cmd.py` already renders a state for a touch
whose session row is gone — useful precedent for the mirror case.

**2. The read-path audit — the bulk of the work.** Queries that today drop
dangling references via inner join will start matching the retained row, so a
removed entity leaks into listings unless each read filters on `removed`. Known
sites include `session_status.go` in internal monitor at lines 184, 349 and 480.
The full sweep covers CLI listings, session status, the monitor, `session next`,
the web dashboard, and the four consumers `session_tasks`,
`session_hidden_tasks`, `session_notices` and `project_next_tasks`/`_pending`.

**3. Drop pending notices in the same removal path.** Delete `session_notices`
rows with `notified = 0` for the removed task rather than filtering them —
an undelivered notice about a removed task is dead mail that would otherwise sit
in the queue permanently. Delivered notice history is unaffected. This is not an
exception to the id rule: a notice's own id is an internal row handle nobody
holds.

## Rebuild check

Confirm the db-ledger projector replays a removal as a retained `removed=1` row.
If it ever replayed removal as a real delete, a rebuild would re-free the id and
reuse would return on a path nobody would think to test.

## From the description

Junction rows whose surrogate PK nobody holds stay hard deletes.

The bulk of the work is the read-path audit: queries that today drop dangling references via inner join start matching the retained row, so every read must filter on removed or a removed entity leaks into a listing.

fields.title: Extend the never-reuse-an-id policy to every non-task entity
fields.description: Extend the never-reuse-an-ID rule beyond tasks by auditing every delete path for entities that mint IDs and converting each hard delete to a removed flag, or confirming none exists.
fields.context:
Per ED-1547, no entity id is ever reused, for any entity type — not just tasks.

Sessions are the known live exposure: session_tasks.session_id is FK-free in exactly the way task_id is, task_cmd already renders a state for a touch whose session row is gone, and the dead-pane reaper work in E-1898 is in that neighborhood.
fields.analysis: Deliverable is a per-entity table of delete paths with each one either converted or documented as absent.

fields.title: Drop pending session notices when their task is removed
fields.description: Drop a removed task's session notices still pending delivery instead of filtering them on read, leaving already-delivered notice history untouched.
fields.notes: Depends on the removed flag existing (E-1929).
fields.context: Per ED-1547, this is the one exception to the filter-everywhere rule for removed rows.
fields.analysis:
An undelivered notice about a removed task is dead mail: filtering it on read leaves it in the queue permanently,

Scope is only notices still pending delivery — already-delivered notice history is unaffected.

fields.title: Purge old session rows now attached to a reused task ID
fields.description: Purge rows written before IDs stopped being reused that now attach to a different task, identified by a row timestamp older than the current task's creation time.
fields.context: The removed=1 policy (ED-1547) is prospective. Rows written before it that key on an id since re-minted are already attached to the wrong task and stay wrong.
fields.analysis:
They are detectable: every one of the four tables carries a timestamp — session_tasks.created_at, session_hidden_tasks.hidden_at, session_notices.changed_at, project_next_tasks.added_at — so a row whose timestamp predates tasks.created_at of the id's current occupant provably belongs to a previous occupant.

then decide whether the check earns a permanent home in the E-1915 reconcile repair or is a one-shot migration.

Note project_next_tasks.task_id is TEXT while the others are INTEGER, so the join needs a cast.

fields.title: Decide whether to keep or retire task import
fields.description: Decide whether to keep endless task import, which loads plan files or JSON as tasks, or retire it along with its bulk task deletion and source-file tracking.
fields.context:
Surfaced while planning E-1929, which has to carry the import path through the removed-flag change.

'endless task import' loads a Claude plan file or JSON into the DB, with --replace bulk-clearing prior tasks from the same source file.

It looks dormant: all 14 tasks with a source_file date from April 2026 across two plan files, 13 of the 14 are declined, and task.bulk_cleared has fired 5 times in the project's entire history.

Plan attachment via 'task update --text' appears to have replaced the workflow it was built for.

Note the CLI is 'task import --json', not the 'task import-json' named in a stale code comment.

fields.title: Block time-frozen specifics from durable task content
fields.description: Block line-number citations in task descriptions and plans, extend the no-time-frozen-specifics rule to all durable task content, and have the guide say to cite file and function names.
fields.context:
ED-1073 already forbids time-frozen specifics — byte counts, file sizes, line numbers, sha hashes — and says to cite file or function names instead so the reader re-locates at pickup. It is violated routinely because nothing enforces it and two things undercut it: ED-1073's own text scopes the rule to the analysis field, so a literal reading does not reach a plan in text, a description, or an outcome; and the tasks guide describes text as a full implementation plan 'including approach, file paths, verification steps', which invites the thing the decision forbids.

Prompted by E-1929's plan, which cited line numbers throughout and goes stale as soon as anything else lands.
fields.analysis:
Settled design, from working through it with Mike. Part 2 of the original
description is already done: ED-1073 was widened the same morning E-1934 was
filed and now reads "no time-frozen specifics in any durable field", enumerating
description, analysis, text/plan, outcome and decision bodies. What remains is
the gate (part 1) and the guide wording (part 3).

## Rule 3 — line citations

`_guard_inline_content` has Rule 1 (whole value is a path token) and Rule 2 (an
absolute path token anywhere). Rule 3 refuses a line citation.

- Matches `<name>.<ext>:<digits>` where `<ext>` is in the citation-extension
  set. Also `<name>.<ext>:<digits>-<digits>` (range) and
  `<name>.<ext>:<digits>:<digits>` (line:col).
- Does NOT match a bare leading-colon number. Nobody writes a bare line number
  that way, and the false positives are everywhere: clock times, host:port,
  ratios.
- Skips any token preceded by a scheme separator or an at-sign, or beginning
  with a www prefix. This is what keeps host:port out of the gate, and it is
  load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces: many source extensions ARE ccTLDs
  (Serbia, Paraguay, Poland, Saint Helena, Mali, Cocos, Moldova), so the
  extension set alone does not separate a file citation from a domain.
- No escape hatch. Rule 2 has one; Rule 3 does not.
- Applies wherever Rule 2 applies: description, text/plan, analysis, outcome and
  decision bodies. E-1992 collapses these into task_content, at which point the
  gate stops enumerating flags and guards content.

## Configuration

Three keys under a content block in the project config file, which already
carries list-valued keys, so no new shape is needed.

- A built-in default extension set of roughly eighty entries covering systems,
  JVM and .NET, scripting, JS/TS and web, functional, data and config, docs,
  and build and schema files.
- Two thin override lists layered over that default rather than replacing it,
  so a project adding or removing one extension does not restate eighty. Named
  `content.extensions.block` and `content.extensions.unblock`, nested. The verb
  attaches to the behaviour rather than to set membership, which is what makes
  it readable a year later: block names one more extension whose citations are
  refused, unblock stops refusing one the default covers. Earlier candidates
  spelled around an abstract "set the gate matches" and every one of them was
  ambiguous in one direction or the other.
- An extension listed in BOTH lists is a config error and must be refused at
  load, not silently resolved. That follows the house pattern already set by
  --clear against a field flag, and by --status against --keep-status: when two
  settings spell contradictory intent, refuse and say so.
- A switch that disables the gate outright, for a project that finds it more
  trouble than it is worth, nested alongside as `content.extensions` sits under
  `content`. Worth giving Rule 2 its own switch at the same time, by the same
  reasoning.

## Widening the built-in path exemption

`_builtin_allowed_dirs` exempts endless's own config and cache directories, and
its docstring already anticipates being extended at that composition point.
Widen it to any dot-directory directly under home. Rule 2's stated rationale is
that absolute paths are non-portable and that a temp path dies with the
worktree; neither is true of a tool's conventional dot-directory under home,
which names the same location for every user on every machine. Home-relative
paths that are NOT dot-directories stay refused — a personal projects directory
really is machine-specific. Encountered live: writing a lesson about the Claude
transcript directory was refused, and the text had to be degraded to prose that
named no location.

## Part 3 — guide wording

The tasks guide still describes text as a full implementation plan "including
approach, file paths, verification steps", which invites the thing ED-1073
forbids, and says nothing about line numbers anywhere. Fix the wording to say
file and function names.

## From the description

Three parts: extend the content gate that already refuses absolute paths in --description/--text so it also refuses file.ext:NNN and bare :NNN citations; widen ED-1073 to govern all durable content; and fix the guide's wording to say file and function names.

fields.title: Make db-ledger rebuild trustworthy over the main DB
fields.description: Make rebuilding the database from the ledger robust and reliable enough to trust over the main database, which a multi-developer setup depends on.
fields.notes: existing candidates include E-1671 and E-1674 (event upcasting so old events replay into the current schema), E-1728 (projector failing task_landings inserts), E-1716 (committed test-fixture ledger events), E-1883 (DB scoping so a rebuild is project-safe), and executor/projector parity testing in general. Relate or reparent those once the shape is agreed.
fields.context:
Today the main DB is canonical and rebuild-db is not trusted: a rebuild is neither robust nor reliable, so it must not be exercised against real data, and verify scripts have to route around it.

That is a load-bearing gap — the ledger is supposed to be the source of truth the DB projects from, and E-1829's two-developer milestone depends on each developer rebuilding the projection from the shared ledger. Until rebuild is trustworthy, every executor handler has a projector twin that nothing exercises end to end, so divergence between them is invisible until someone rebuilds and loses data.

fields.title: Decide how sessions and background jobs message each other
fields.description: Decide what inter-session messaging Endless should have, covering interactive sessions and background workers, weighing Claude Code's messaging tool and the MCP standard as candidates.
fields.notes: the 2026-08-14 research brief is now tracked at docs/arch-2026-08-14-cross-session-messaging.md (it was under docs/private, excluded via .git/info/exclude and so absent from every worktree and every other clone).
fields.context: Claude Code's SendMessage tool and the recently-changed MCP standard are the leading candidates;
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

## Why this is being asked now

E-1898 rebuilt session→pane binding onto a `processes` table keyed on
`(kind, server_uuid, address)`, because the old `sessions.process` string (a
bare tmux pane id) is not unique across tmux server lifetimes — the root cause
of the 2026-08-05 incident that nulled live pane bindings project-wide.

`channels` keys on that SAME string (`INSERT INTO channels (process, port, pid,
created_at)`, `DELETE FROM channels WHERE process=?`, `SELECT port, pid FROM
channels WHERE process=?` — internal/monitor/session.go). E-1898
deliberately left it alone rather than migrate a surface believed dead, so
after E-1898 lands `channels` is the last consumer of the old non-unique key.

## The assumption that needs confirming first

"channels is vestigial" is Mike's read, and it may be wrong. The
`endless-channel` MCP server is still wired into live Claude sessions — its
instructions ship in the session system prompt:

    Events from Endless arrive as <channel source="endless-channel" ...>.
    When you see event_type="message", run: endless channel inbox

So the surface is at minimum still *installed*. Whether it is ever *exercised*
is the empirical question.

## What to brainstorm

1. **Confirm the premise.** Does anything read/write `channels`? Is the MCP
   server ever actually invoked? Check the ledger, the errors log, and whether
   any session has ever run `endless channel inbox` unprompted.

2. **Re-read the MCP standard.** It has changed recently; capabilities that
   were impossible when endless-channel was built may now be available.
   Reference Mike watched: https://youtube.com/watch?v=oqp6D-ugtX4

3. **Evaluate `SendMessage`.** Claude Code exposes a SendMessage tool that
   continues a previously spawned agent by ID/name with its context intact.
   That may be a better transport for inter-session communication than a
   bespoke MCP server plus a port/pid table — it needs no listener, no port
   allocation, and no process-keyed row that can go stale.

4. **Decide.** Three live options:
   - retire `channels` + the MCP server outright;
   - migrate `channels.process` onto `processes.process_id` (only worth it if
     the surface is genuinely used);
   - rebuild inter-session comms on SendMessage and retire the rest.

## Out of scope

Implementation. The outcome is a decision plus a follow-on retirement or
design task.

## From the description

Scope includes background workers, not just interactive sessions: triage jobs are intended to be able to communicate with sessions. Out of scope: the fate of the existing channel surface, which is dead and is being removed under its own task -- this brainstorm is about the replacement, not the retirement, and neither blocks the other.

fields.description: Decode text stored as binary blobs when reading from the database, so task show --text and other readers get strings instead of crashing on bytes.
fields.notes: Extends E-1914, which set a lenient text_factory in get_conn for the same failure shape;

One value in the ledger is affected (tasks.text for E-449), from an importer that no longer exists — no live writer to fix.

fields.description: Excise the proof-of-concept web dashboard along with its build toolchain and web-only dependencies, which nothing else in Endless needs.
fields.notes: See analysis for the inspected scope.
fields.analysis:
Remove the web dashboard entirely. It is a proof-of-concept that will not be
evolved: web work was deliberately halted to focus on the harder database,
hooks, and workflow problems, and every task targeting it has been obsoleted.
Keeping it costs a whole build toolchain and dependency surface that nothing
else in Endless needs.

Scope by inspection, to be re-verified at implementation time rather than
trusted from this description:

- The `internal/web` package tree (components, pages, templates, data, static,
  assets) and `internal/servecmd`, which is its only caller.
- The `serve` subcommand dispatch in the Go entrypoint, and the Python `serve`
  command that shells out to it including its port option and binary-watch
  restart loop.
- Justfile recipes and their invocations from the aggregate build: templ
  generation, the tailwind CSS build, the templUI symlink helper, and the dev
  watcher recipes that run them. The aggregate build recipe and the help text
  both name these and must stop doing so.
- Go module requirements that exist only for the web stack: the templ runtime
  and templUI. Check goldmark separately — the terminal renderer in
  `internal/mdterm` uses it independently and must keep working. Re-vendor
  after pruning.
- Tracked generated artifacts: the `*_templ.go` files and the built CSS output.
  Also the land-time handling that exists because these are build-regenerated
  and git-tracked.
- External tooling assumptions: templ and tailwindcss as prerequisites for
  building the project.

Verify afterward that a clean build, the full test suite, and vendoring all
succeed with the web toolchain absent, and that no remaining code imports the
removed packages. `internal/mdterm` carries a comment describing itself in
terms of the web markdown renderer; reword it so it does not reference a
package that no longer exists.

Deliberately out of scope: anything about a future web UI. When a web surface
is wanted again it will be preceded by research into whether Endless should
host it at all or whether a different tool should, with Endless integrating.
Do not file follow-on work for that here.

## From the description

It is a proof-of-concept that will not be evolved: web work was deliberately halted to focus on the harder database, hooks, and workflow problems, and every task targeting it has been obsoleted. Keeping it costs a whole build toolchain (templ generation, tailwind CSS, templUI) and dependency surface that nothing else in Endless needs.

Scope covers the internal/web package tree, internal/servecmd and its only caller, the Go and Python serve commands, the justfile recipes and their invocations from the aggregate build, the web-only Go module requirements, and the tracked generated artifacts.

Out of scope: anything about a future web UI.

fields.title: Fix landed-state detection reporting a false all-clear
fields.description: Fix worktree settled detection to rely on the recorded landing, report unknown instead of settled when its git checks fail, and stop assuming the default branch is main.
fields.notes: See analysis.
fields.context:
'I could not tell' is rendered identically to 'you are clear'.

The rev-list probe also hardcodes 'main', which exits 128 on any project whose default branch differs, so those projects show a permanent false all-clear and the marker can never appear.

fields.title: Rework just land's ordering so the DB never leads the code
fields.description: Rework the order of steps in just land so no failure leaves the database migrated ahead of the installed binary, checking the worktree's source is current with main before building.
fields.notes: Analysis carries the full sequence.
fields.context:
Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 produced two failures in the land recipe itself.

First, `just land` rebuilds the worktree binary but never checks the worktree's SOURCE is current with main, so a branch 147 commits behind rebuilt a still-stale binary and aborted on an unrelated enum-drift error naming gate_kinds. Second — and the expensive one — apply-change then SUCCEEDED and the merge failed, leaving the real database migrated to a schema no installed binary understood; session tracking froze machine-wide and recovery needed a manual restore.

The justfile only reasons about apply FAILING ("the land aborts before main advances"); apply succeeding and the merge failing is the unhandled, irreversible case.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

One root cause with four faces: **code and database versions diverge across the
worktree / main / real-ledger boundary, and nothing guards the seam.** All four
were hit for real on 2026-08-10, in one sitting, landing E-1898.

## Face 1 — the land uses a binary built from stale source

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 came from E-1709, whose comment names this failure: "A worktree rebased
onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE binary whose
embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664 guard only
checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half. It makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE. Nothing
makes the source match MAIN. With the branch 147 commits behind, `just go`
faithfully rebuilt a still-stale binary and step 2 hit the same wall:

    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id="2" slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds. Main's E-1901 had added `GateKindRelay` and
applied the row; the worktree's source predated it. The rebase that would fix
this is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Face 2 — apply-change succeeds, the merge fails, the DB is left ahead

After rebasing by hand, the land was re-run. This time step 2 SUCCEEDED and the
land then failed, so main never got the code. Result: the real DB was migrated
to a schema only the unlanded branch understands, while every installed binary
still expected the old one. Every session query referenced a dropped column, so
all 64 sessions went unresolvable and session tracking froze machine-wide (0
writes in the following 7 minutes).

The justfile comment asserts: "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances (clean recovery)." It reasons only about apply FAILING. Apply
succeeding and the merge then failing is the unhandled — and worse — case,
because it is the one that is irreversible.

## Face 3 — no supported way back (SPLIT OUT to E-1942)

`endless db backup` exists and the land calls it. There is no `endless db
restore`. Recovery was an unguided `cp`, and it went wrong twice:

- Copied over a live database with six open connections, leaving a hot
  `endless.db-journal`. A read-only connection cannot roll back a hot journal,
  so every reader returned `database is locked` and the status bar flickered.
- The backup is produced by `VACUUM INTO`, which writes a **rollback-journal**
  database. The live DB was WAL. Restoring silently changed journal mode, and
  every connection then fought over an exclusive lock to switch it back.

Recovery took: `pkill -f 'endless task show'` (four abandoned pagers holding
connections for up to 22 days), killing two `session-status --monitor`
processes, then `sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'`
to roll back the journal and restore WAL. None of that is discoverable.

A backup you cannot safely restore is not insurance.

## Face 4 — MOVED to E-1944

The worktree's Claude hook runs candidate code against the real ledger (E-998
points the hook at the candidate binary; E-1450 forces hooks to the real DB).
That pair is safe only while the schema is unchanged, and deciding it means
deciding who may define, migrate and use the schema — which is E-1944. It is
out of scope HERE so this task stays spawnable.

## Decided approach

**Face 1 — refuse, do not auto-rebase.** Before rebuilding the worktree binary,
refuse the land when `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0, telling the user to
rebase. Auto-rebasing mid-land is rejected: E-1898's own rebase stopped on a
conflict in the append-only db-ledger JSONL, and a rebase that stalls with main
partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

**Face 2 — rehearse the merge, then reorder.** Do the merge on a throwaway
branch first (`endless-land-<taskid>-<rand>`, removed in a trap, so concurrent
lands cannot collide):

  1. branch off main, merge/rebase the task branch onto it
  2. it fails -> delete the branch, abort. The DB was never touched.
  3. it succeeds -> FAST-FORWARD main to that result. A pointer move, so there
     is no window where main advances and something else does not. Do NOT redo
     the merge; re-merging reopens the gap it just closed.
  4. THEN apply the schema changes, then record the landing, then rebuild.

Applying AFTER the fast-forward inverts the asymmetry that caused the incident:

  - apply fails after the merge -> main has the code, the DB lacks the
    migration. Re-run `endless db apply-change`; it is idempotent and gated by
    `_schema_version`. Recoverable.
  - merge fails after apply -> what happened on 2026-08-10. Not recoverable
    without a restore.

**Diagnosis, independent of the above.** Every `VerifyIntegrity` call site can
name the likely cause when the DB has rows the binary lacks: "this binary
predates the database; rebase onto main and rebuild." That direction of drift is
always staleness, never corruption. The reverse (binary has constants the DB
lacks) is a genuinely missing migration and should keep reading as it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself, which is fixed and re-verified. `endless task show -p` pinning a
DB connection for the life of its pager is a real but separate nuisance; file it
on its own if it bites again.

## From the description

Fix: refuse the land when the branch is behind main, rehearse the merge on a throwaway branch, fast-forward main to that result, and apply schema changes AFTER the merge so a failed apply is merely a retry.

fields.description: Add endless db restore, which safely restores the database from a backup, handling open connections and journal modes, instead of recovering by hand-copying files.
fields.context:
`endless db backup` exists and `just land` calls it, but there is no way to USE a backup — recovery is an unguided `cp`.

On 2026-08-10 that went wrong twice: copying over a database with six open connections left a hot journal that made every reader fail with 'database is locked', and `VACUUM INTO` backups are rollback-journal while the live DB is WAL, so connections then fought over switching it back.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

## Why this is needed

`just land` takes a backup before applying a schema change, so the safety net is
already half-built. The other half does not exist: there is no way to use it.

On 2026-08-10 a land applied E-1898's migration to the real ledger and then
failed before merging, leaving the database on a schema no installed binary
understood. Session tracking froze machine-wide. Recovery was an ad-hoc `cp`,
and it went wrong twice before it went right:

1. **Copied over a live database.** Six connections were open (two
   `session-status --monitor`, four `endless task show -p` abandoned in pagers
   for up to 22 days). That left a hot `endless.db-journal`. A read-only
   connection cannot roll back a hot journal, so every reader returned
   `database is locked` and the tmux status bar flickered on and off.

2. **Journal mode silently changed.** `endless db backup` uses `VACUUM INTO`,
   which writes a **rollback-journal** database. The live DB was WAL. After the
   restore every connection fought for an exclusive lock trying to switch back.

What finally worked, none of it discoverable:

    pkill -f 'endless task show'          # abandoned pagers holding connections
    kill <session-status --monitor pids>
    sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'

## What the verb should do

`endless db restore [<backup>]` — default to the most recent backup.

1. Refuse unless the target is a real Endless DB and the backup opens clean.
2. Enumerate open connections (the equivalent of `lsof` on the db file) and
   REPORT them by pid and command. Do not kill anything silently; either refuse
   with the list, or require an explicit flag to proceed.
3. Restore the file.
4. Re-establish `journal_mode=WAL` and run `PRAGMA integrity_check`, failing
   loudly if it is not `ok`.
5. Keep the pre-restore database aside (timestamped) so the restore itself is
   reversible.

## Notes

- Step 2 is the load-bearing one. Every failure above came from copying over a
  file other processes had open, not from the copy itself.
- A dry-run mode that prints what it would do (holders, journal mode, sizes)
  costs little and is what you actually want at 5am mid-incident.
- Related: E-1941 covers the land-flow ordering that creates the need for a
  restore in the first place. This task is the recovery tool; that one is the
  prevention. They are independent — the tool is worth having regardless.

## From the description

that defaults to the newest backup, REPORTS open connections by pid/command rather than killing them silently, keeps the pre-restore file aside, and afterwards re-establishes WAL and runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` failing loudly on anything but 'ok'. A dry-run mode printing holders and journal mode is what you actually want mid-incident.

fields.title: Decide how worktree branches survive a rewrite of main
fields.description: Decide how worktree branches keep a usable base when main's history is rewritten under them, so Endless works whether or not git pulls rebase.
fields.notes: Analysis carries the evidence.
fields.context:
Worktree branches lose their base when main's history is rewritten under them — not from amending.

canAmend already refuses to amend a tip another ref can reach, but implements that as SHA reachability, so once `git pull --rebase` rewrites main the guard answers a question the rewrite made meaningless, permits the amend, and the land rebase then conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.
fields.analysis:
Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as new events append, so the
tip commit's SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those
SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main holds
equivalent (superset) content under a different SHA, and the branch still
points at the superseded one. On land, the rebase replays the orphan and
conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.

`_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` (E-1342) already handles this for a
contiguous run of orphans at the branch base. Its docstring puts mid-branch
orphans out of scope deliberately: a non-amendable commit followed by an
amendable one only arose from pre-E-1309 contamination, and dropping a
mid-branch commit risks deleting intended work. The open question is what to do
when that assumption no longer holds.

Observed on the e-801 worktree. Its branch reflog showed `Created from main`
with no commits of its own before the session's, yet `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its commits as patch-equivalent to commits on main —
the inherited run of amended ledger commits. The land reported dropping base
auto-amend commits and then conflicted anyway, so the existing helper did not
cover this shape. Recovery-and-retry could not converge because each replayed
ledger commit conflicts in turn.

Two framings, and the choice between them is the point of this brainstorm.

Treat it as a rebase problem, and the levers are: widen the E-1342 helper past
contiguous-at-base once it can distinguish an inherited orphan from real work;
detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis rather
than discovering it mid-conflict; give the ledger segments a union merge driver
so concurrent appends stop conflicting; or reset a branch onto main when its
base is known-orphaned and only its own commits need replaying.

Treat it as a commit-shape problem, and the lever is upstream of all of that:
amending a commit that other refs may be built on is what manufactures the
orphans. Appending a new ledger commit instead of amending would cost more
commits on main but leave every fork point stable. Whether the amend behavior
earns its keep, and what it was buying, needs establishing before the rebase-side
options are worth ranking.

Two gaps are evidence rather than separate tasks, since their fix depends on
which framing wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.

Relates to E-1941, a different failure from the same root condition: `just
land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from still-stale worktree
source, because the rebase onto main runs afterward.

A correction worth keeping, because it cost this session three wrong
conclusions: commit counts mislead here. A branch can read as hundreds of
commits ahead while being an ancestor of main in content. `git cherry` and a
tree comparison tell the truth; `git reflog show <branch>` tells you where the
branch actually came from, which is what finally identified the cause.

## Root cause identified: `pull.rebase=true` blinds canAmend's guard (E-1941 session, 2026-08-11)

The orphan is not produced by amending per se. `canAmend`
(internal/events/commit.go) already refuses to amend a tip another ref
can reach — precondition 2, "HEAD must not be reachable from any ref BESIDES the
current branch." A worktree branch forked from main's ledger tip normally
triggers that refusal and endless appends instead. The commit-shape lever this
brainstorm proposes is therefore already implemented; the question is why it did
not fire.

Because it implements reachability as a SHA test: `git for-each-ref --contains
HEAD`. `git pull --rebase` rewrites every local main commit to a new SHA. The
task branch still points into the old, now-unreachable SHAs, so it no longer
"contains" main's HEAD. The guard is not bypassed and does not error — it
answers a reachability question the rewrite made meaningless, returns "safe to
amend," and the next amend diverges main from every task branch.

Reproduced with a harness that re-implements precondition 2 faithfully (the
`for-each-ref --contains HEAD` test, skipping the current branch) and reports
its decision either side of a pull:

    G1  no pull:          guard -> APPEND (saw refs/heads/task/900)   land: OK
    G2  after git pull:   guard -> AMEND  (saw no other ref)          land: CONFLICT
                                          conflicts: .endless/db-ledger/seg.jsonl

Mike set `pull.rebase true` manually at repo scope on 2026-08-10. main's reflog
carries the resulting rewrite: `e3ef6acb main@{2026-08-10 05:07:46}: rebase
(finish): refs/heads/main onto 43f238a9`, ~330 commits, about 3.5 hours before
E-1941 was filed. `pull.rebase=false` preserves local SHAs (it adds a merge
commit), so the guard keeps working — the merge strategy is an unstated,
load-bearing precondition of a safety check, not a style preference. Mike's ask
is that endless support either setting.

Consequences for the levers listed above:

- **The union merge driver for ledger segments must be struck.** It would
  corrupt the ledger. `Event` (internal/events/event.go) carries no unique
  id, and neither `ReadAllEvents` nor the projector dedups; union merge's defining
  behavior is to keep both sides' lines in a conflicted region, manufacturing
  duplicate entries that replay double-applies. `verbs.jsonl` tolerates union only
  because `matchers._add_verb_to_file` dedups at load. It also contradicts
  standing policy: land Step 3.75 refuses branch-side ledger commits and E-1342
  drops orphaned ones, so a merge driver would legitimize the cross-branch ledger
  merging the rest of the system refuses. (`ReadAllEvents` does re-sort by kairos
  TS, so the corruption vector is duplication rather than ordering — that does not
  rescue the idea.)
- **Any fix that stays SHA-reachability-based inherits the bug.** Widening the
  E-1342 helper, or refusing early with a named diagnosis, both still ask "is this
  commit reachable from another ref," which a rewrite answers wrongly. A durable
  fix needs an identity for a fork point that survives a history rewrite, or it
  needs to stop the rewrite from reaching ledger commits.
- **The framing choice may be moot.** This is not "rebase problem vs commit-shape
  problem" — the commit-shape guard exists and is correct; an external history
  rewrite defeats it. The live question is how endless behaves when main's history
  is rewritten under it, under either `pull.rebase` setting.

Also tested and negative, for whoever prices the E-1941 plan: rehearsing the land
on a throwaway branch off main and *merging* the task branch into it conflicts on
the same file, in the same cases, as the current rebase does. Four scenarios were
run (amend alone; pull --rebase alone; both; both with a union driver) against
two strategies — rebase the task branch onto main, versus branch off main and
merge the task branch in — and the two strategies gave an identical verdict in
every one. Changing the merge shape does not help a guard that has gone blind.

## Arguments tried and discarded (E-1941 session, 2026-08-11)

Recorded so this ground is not re-covered. Each of these was argued, tested, and
failed; the first two were mine and wrong.

1. *"The amend causes the conflict; `pull.rebase` does not."* Rested on a harness
   that called `git commit --amend` directly. That bypasses canAmend, so it
   tested a scenario unreachable in real endless — G1 above shows the guard
   refuses exactly that amend. Attributing the cause to the mechanism instead of
   to what disables the mechanism inverted the diagnosis. The pull is the cause.

2. *"Give the ledger segments a `merge=union` driver."* Listed as a lever in this
   analysis and briefly recommended as the fix. It would corrupt the ledger: no
   event identity, no dedup on the read path, so union's duplicate lines
   double-apply on replay. Struck above with the full reasoning.

3. *"Merge instead of rebase, so the orphan is never replayed."* The most
   plausible reading of the E-1941 plan's "branch off main, merge/rebase the task
   branch onto it," and the strongest remaining case for the throwaway rehearsal
   branch. Tested and false — merge conflicts identically, because the merge-base
   still sits behind the amend, so both sides have touched the append region.

4. *"Endless never runs `git pull` itself, so no code path branches on the
   setting."* True and irrelevant. The user runs `git pull`. A safety guard that
   silently degrades under a standard git setting has the defect regardless of
   who types the command.

What survived: the current land already has the rehearse-then-pointer-move shape
(Step 4 rebases in the worktree with a clean abort; Step 5 is `merge --ff-only`,
a pure pointer move), so E-1941's DB-ahead invariant needs only the apply
reorder, not a new merge mechanism.

## From the description

Endless must work under either `pull.rebase` setting: rebase-style pull is mainstream, and a guard that silently degrades under it is a defect regardless of which setting this repo uses.

Any SHA-reachability-based fix inherits the same blindness; the union-merge-driver option is struck (it would corrupt the ledger).

Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks.

fields.title: Decide who may define, migrate, and use the DB schema
fields.description: Decide which binaries may define, migrate and use the database schema, and when, so no binary silently migrates, or runs against, a schema it does not match.
fields.notes: Analysis carries the full state tables.
fields.context:
The 2026-08-10 incident produced four distinct failures from one question.

`monitor.DB()` applies schema.sql on EVERY connection, so any binary additively migrates whatever DB it opens; E-1818's schema-passive mode stops that for pinned surfaces but only protects the DB from the binary, never the binary from the DB — a candidate binary against a main-schema ledger (or vice versa) passes connect cleanly and then fails at runtime writing or reading columns that aren't there.

That is what took session tracking down for 30 minutes.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

Provoked by the 2026-08-10 incident landing E-1898, which produced four distinct
failures in one sitting from one underlying question: **who is allowed to define,
migrate, and use the schema, and when.**

## What governs schema writes today

`monitor.DB()` applies `schema.SQL` — all additive `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` —
on EVERY connection, plus five enum `VerifyIntegrity` gates that fail closed.
Destructive one-off change files run separately, once, at land time via
`endless db apply-change`.

E-1818 added **schema-passive**: when `dbPathOverride != ""` (set by
`PinMainDB`/`ForceRealDB`, i.e. the hook, tmux and channel surfaces) the connect
skips both the schema apply and every gate.

**The gap.** Schema-passive protects the DB from the binary. It does nothing to
protect the binary from the DB. The hook error on 2026-08-10 proves it: the
candidate binary did not migrate anything, it simply failed writing `process_id`
into a table that lacked the column. E-1818 solved one half; the unsolved half
is the one that caused the outage.

## A. What each executable does on connect

| Executable | Surface | Pins real DB? | Applies schema.sql | Runs enum gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| global (main) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| global (main) | task, sql, event, ... | no | yes | yes |
| worktree (candidate) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| worktree (candidate) | event apply-change | no | YES | YES  <- the gate_kinds abort |
| worktree (candidate) | anything with --config-dir | no | yes (that DB) | yes |
| Python CLI | all | n/a | own bootstrap | none |

## B. Binary schema vs. DB schema

| Binary expects | DB has | Connect | Runtime DML | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | main | ok | ok | normal |
| candidate | candidate | ok | ok | sandbox only |
| candidate | main | ok (passive) | FAILS: writes absent columns | hook errors, 30 min |
| main | candidate | ok (passive) | FAILS: reads dropped columns | blank board, 30 min |

Rows 3 and 4 are one defect seen from either side. NEITHER is detected at
connect; both surface as runtime SQL errors on hot paths. The enum gates cover
enum tables only and would never catch a dropped column.

## C. Landing phases

| Phase | Binary | DB | Schema | What failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 rebuild worktree bin | worktree | - | - | built from stale source (147 behind) |
| 2 backup | Python | real | pre | - |
| 3 apply-change | worktree | real | pre -> post | gate abort; later succeeded |
| 4 merge | git | - | - | FAILED -> DB post, code pre |
| 5 record landing | worktree | real | post | never reached |
| 6 just build | - | - | - | never reached; global stayed pre |

## Hypotheses to evaluate

**H1 — a migration-only executable.** Built from the landing branch, does DDL
only, never DML, so it has no runtime schema expectations to be wrong about.
Cleanly resolves phase 3. Does NOT touch table B rows 3/4, which are ordinary
binaries at runtime.

**H2 — explicit upgrade; connects verify instead of migrate.** Replace
apply-on-connect with an `endless db upgrade` verb; ordinary connects compare
the DB's schema version against the binary's and REFUSE with a clear message.
This is the one that collapses table B: rows 3 and 4 become a precise
connect-time refusal, and no binary can mutate the real ledger by opening it —
which also makes schema-passive unnecessary. Costs users an explicit step after
upgrade, and every entry point needs a good "your database needs upgrading"
message.

**Neither resolves everything, and that should be stated up front:**
- Ordering (phase 3 vs 4) is independent — see E-1941. H2 arguably makes a
  half-landed state MORE visibly broken (everything refuses) rather than less.
- Recovery is independent — see E-1942, whose shape depends on this decision:
  "copy a backup back" vs "upgrade --rollback" are different verbs.
- Whether candidate hook code should write to the real ledger at all (the
  E-998 / E-1450 tension) is a policy question this may inform but does not
  answer.

## The tension, named

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's hook at CANDIDATE code so it gets exercised.
E-1450 forces hooks to write to the REAL ledger so activity is real. Each is
correct alone; together they mean unlanded code writes production data, which
is safe exactly while the schema is unchanged and unsafe the moment it is not.

It is not a genuine catch-22. It is unresolvable only while one binary defines,
migrates, and uses the schema at once. Separating define/migrate from use — H1
and H2 together — collapses it.

## Deliverable

A decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies. Not an implementation.



## Folded in from E-1922: the concrete form of H2

E-1922 was filed separately as an implementation of exactly H2's connect-time
check, and is folded here because it presupposes a decision this task has not
yet made. Its evidence stands regardless of which hypothesis wins, and is worth
keeping in front of whoever decides:

`monitor.DB()` executes its embedded schema SQL on every owned connection with
no check that the DB carries the change files that schema assumes. Nothing
connects a binary's expectations to the DB's actual state, so a binary
installed before its change file is applied can create schema objects
referencing columns that do not exist. E-1917's trigger reads
`NEW.changed_by_session`, and SQLite resolves trigger bodies at fire time, so
every `UPDATE tasks` would fail — the failure is not at connect, it is at the
next write, which is what makes it hard to attribute.

Today that is avoided only by convention: land, which runs apply-change, before
`just install`. A convention is not a guard, and the ordering requirement is
invisible to anyone who has not been bitten by it.

E-1922 proposed a gate that either auto-applies pending changes on connect or
refuses with a clear error. Note that those are two different answers, not one:
auto-applying keeps a binary able to migrate whatever DB it opens, which is the
property H1 and H2 are both trying to remove; refusing is H2 proper. If H2 is
chosen, this becomes its first follow-on task. If H1 is chosen instead, the
convention-only ordering requirement still needs an answer, and this evidence
is where that answer starts.

## From the description

Two hypotheses to evaluate: a migration-only executable built from the landing branch that does DDL and never DML; and replacing apply-on-connect with an explicit `endless db upgrade`, with ordinary connects verifying the schema version and refusing rather than silently fixing it.

Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks, not an implementation.

fields.description: Allow task update --status to set submitted like every other agent-settable status, so editing a description and moving the task to submitted take one command.
fields.context: Every other agent-settable status can ride along with a description edit in one call; submitted cannot, so routing a task to submitted after editing its description takes a second command (task submit). That asymmetry is a direct cause of agents leaving edited tasks sitting in untriaged: the one-call path exists for 'needs a plan' but not for 'description is sufficient'.
fields.analysis: Add submitted to the accepted values; task submit stays as the standalone verb.

fields.description: Fix the triager to judge a brainstorm task on whether its problem statement suffices, since its plan is the deliverable, instead of routing it to unplanned for lacking a plan.
fields.context:
The triager routed E-1943 (type brainstorm, description plus full analysis, no plan attached) to unplanned.

The triager appears to apply the same plan-attached heuristic across all task types.
fields.analysis:
For a brainstorm the plan IS the deliverable, so 'no plan attached' can never mean 'needs a plan first' — a brainstorm whose problem statement is sufficient should route to submitted and be spawnable.

Make the routing type-aware: for brainstorm, judge whether the problem statement and constraints are sufficient to explore from, not whether a plan exists.

Check research tasks for the same mis-read, since their deliverable is the outcome rather than a plan.

fields.title: Add reap's live-session guards to worktree drop
fields.description: Add to worktree drop both guards reap already has, refusing to remove a worktree that a live session is bound to or that a live process is sitting in.
fields.notes: that is left to E-1902, which replaces it with warn+snapshot+proceed. Coordinate with E-1898 and E-1941.
fields.context:
hit for real, recovered only by mkdir'ing the directory back.

Two+ weeks were previously lost to designs that deleted worktrees on landing, so this is high-severity.

Drop today checks only foreign state and uncommitted changes.

Drop's docstring also promises an unlanded refusal it never performs;
fields.analysis:
# Both halves of "don't drop a worktree someone is standing in"

Folded together per ED-1550: the gate and the guidance are two symptoms of one
cause, and shipping either alone leaves the failure reachable.

## Half 1 — the code gate (the original scope)

Drop checks only foreign state and uncommitted changes. Reap checks more, and
drop should adopt both of its guards:

| Guard | Location | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| Non-ended session row with `active_task_id` for the task | `reap_worktrees.go` | a bound Claude session whose cwd has moved out temporarily |
| `hasLiveProcessInDir` (`lsof -d cwd +D`) | `reap_worktrees.go` | any process standing in the directory right now |

Either alone leaves a hole. The `lsof` probe misses a session that stepped out;
the session-table probe misses a non-Claude process. Given the severity, take
both.

## Half 2 — the guidance (folded in from a separate filing, 2026-08-16)

Twice recently sessions ADVISED dropping a worktree whose git history had
diverged from main, when no committed work would be lost and a reset or rebase
was the correct move. Dropping deletes the directory out from under the live
Claude session and orphans it — the failure class that previously cost two-plus
weeks of recovery.

A gate stops the damage but not the advice, and an agent blocked by a guard
still needs to know what to do instead — otherwise the refusal just becomes a
thing to work around. So this task must ALSO state the reset-versus-drop
decision in the agent-facing guidance: the worktree guide section and the spawn
handoff. Name the correct move before the destructive one is reachable.

Coordinate with the handoff-doc work already in flight, and with E-1898 and
E-1941, still moving through this code.

## Deliberately NOT in scope

Drop's docstring also promises an unlanded refusal the implementation never

## From the description

Drop must adopt BOTH guards reap already has, not just one: (a) reap_worktrees.go refuses when a non-ended session row has active_task_id for the task — catches a bound Claude session whose cwd moved; (b) reap_worktrees.go hasLiveProcessInDir refuses when any process holds cwd inside the dir — catches a session sitting in it.

Scope is these two guards.

fields.title: Make status routing read as the agent's job
fields.description: Make CLI messages and docs present choosing a task's status after a description edit as the agent's own routing decision, not a system outcome to route around.
fields.context:
Agents repeatedly narrate 'this sends it back through triage' after a description edit, treating the reset as a system outcome to route around rather than a routing call to make.

Three things teach that. CLAUDE.md documents triage running automatically, which reads as exclusivity — the mechanism gives an agent nothing actionable and invites deferral. task update's transition message offers only --keep-status to suppress, never naming the decision. And task update --status rejects 'submitted', so the one-call path exists for 'needs a plan' but not for 'the description is sufficient', making the right answer the harder one to reach.
fields.analysis: Fix all three: accept submitted in --status (task submit stays as the standalone verb), reword the transition message to lead with DECIDE YOURSELF and name the background sweep as a worst-case fallback, and drop the automation mechanics from CLAUDE.md — agents need the duty, not the machinery.

fields.title: Explore how a self-dev session reports Endless blocking it
fields.description: Explore how an agent tells the user in chat when Endless blocks something that should work, treating that friction as product feedback instead of silently working around it.
fields.context:
When an agent using Endless hits something that should work but does not, the reflex is to work around it silently and keep going — the user never learns the product blocked them.

Observed this session: task update --status rejected submitted, and the workaround (a second task submit call) was applied without comment until asked.
fields.analysis:
In self_dev mode especially the agent is a user of the product, and its friction is product signal.

Reporting means TELLING THE USER IN CHAT, not filing a task — auto-filing would raise the file-to-close ratio this is partly meant to protect.

Decide: what counts as blocked-but-should-work versus an ordinary error, how the agent phrases it inline without derailing the task at hand, how to keep it from becoming noise, and whether it applies only under self_dev or to any project.

fields.title: Redesign task report around partial success
fields.description: Redesign task report to accept valid fields when others are rejected and keep state between runs, so a rejected or missing field no longer costs a whole extra invocation.
fields.context:
`task report` renders a report in one shot with no partial success and no persisted state, so any rejected or absent field costs a whole extra invocation —

one turn of an E-1939 session needed three calls to emit one block. A rejected note discards the valid `verify` field with it; the statelessness is undiscoverable given the id-addressed, payload-taking surface; a bare run at `unverified` asserts `Nothing to report.` for a task whose handoff mandates a verify command; and the PostToolUse hook fires on `--help`.
fields.analysis:
`task report` models a report as a one-shot render with no partial success and
no persisted state, so any rejected or absent field costs a full extra
invocation. One task rather than four: the symptoms below share that cause.

Evidence — one turn of an E-1939 session took three calls to emit one block:

1. ALL-OR-NOTHING VALIDATION. A payload of {verify, notes} had its note bounced
   by the ceremony check, and the command emitted NO block at all — the valid
   `verify` field was discarded alongside the rejected note. Rendering the block
   from the accepted fields, plus a rejection notice naming what was dropped and
   why, would have made this the last call instead of the middle one.

   The check's judgment was CORRECT: the note recounted a rebase and its
   conflict resolution, which a reviewer can read off the commits. The defect is
   the blast radius of a rejection, not the rejection itself.

2. STATELESSNESS IS UNDISCOVERABLE. The command is addressed by task id, takes a
   structured payload, and sits beside `task update` / `task submit`, which
   persist. It does not persist — a payload supplied in one call is gone by the
   next. The session spent a call running it bare to find that out. Either
   persist the payload on the task, or make the one-shot nature evident in the
   help text and the `--json` option description.

3. AN EMPTY BLOCK AT `unverified` IS NEAR-CERTAINLY WRONG. Run bare on a task
   just flipped to `unverified`, it prints `Nothing to report.` — for a task
   whose handoff mandates a verify command. It cannot know that command, but it
   does know the status and that no `verify` entry was passed, so it can say so
   rather than assert a null result the handoff forbids.

4. THE PostToolUse HOOK FIRES ON `--help`. Running `task report --help` to look
   up the `--json` shape injects the full "now append the block, unchanged,
   after the separator" instruction when no block was rendered. The hook matches
   the command name rather than a successful render.

Deliberately out of scope: the ceremony check's judgment criteria. They are
working, and loosening them to reduce round-trips would trade a real quality
gate for a cheap one.

## From the description

Filed as one task because all four share that root cause.
