fields.title: Refuse a ledger amend when a task branch holds that tree
fields.description: Refuse to amend a ledger commit whose ledger content any task branch tip already holds identically, alongside the existing reachability check that a rewrite of main defeats.
fields.notes: Implements ED-1553;
fields.analysis:
# Reproduction harness (E-1943)

Self-contained. Simulates canAmend's precondition 2 faithfully and, under
LEDGER_ID_TEST=1, the proposed content-identity precondition. Proves the idea;
does NOT exercise real endless code — E-1955's verify script must do that.

Results:

    SHA guard only (today)                     + content-identity test
    S1 no pull, ledger (guard)      land=OK    land=OK
    S2 pull --rebase, ledger        land=CONFLICT   land=OK  (saw task/900 by content)
    S3 pull --rebase, no more       land=OK    land=OK
    S4 pull --rebase, forced append land=OK    land=OK
    S5 pull --merge, ledger         land=OK    land=OK
    S6 no pull, no more             land=OK    land=OK
    S7 rebase, append once, +5      land=OK    land=OK  (amend resumed)
    S8 rebase, guard only,  +5      land=CONFLICT   land=OK  (amend resumed)
    S9 rebase, append once, +20     land=OK    land=OK  (amend resumed)

S8 is the load-bearing one: after the single suppressed amend, the guard
returns to amending and the land stays clean — the fix self-releases.

Run: `LEDGER_ID_TEST=0 bash harness.sh` then `LEDGER_ID_TEST=1 bash harness.sh`

## Script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# E-1943 harness: does `git pull --rebase` alone break a land, or only pull+amend?
#
# Re-implements canAmend precondition 1+2 (subject match; for-each-ref --contains
# HEAD skipping the current branch), reports its decision, then attempts land's
# rebase and reports OK / CONFLICT.
set -uo pipefail

ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$ROOT"' EXIT

LEDGER=".endless/db-ledger/db-entries-aaaa-000001.jsonl"
SUBJ="Endless: record ledger entry"
DECISION=""
SAW=""
N=0
TAIL=0

g() { git -C "$@"; }

can_amend() {
  local repo head_subj cur_ref refs r
  repo="$1"
  head_subj="$(git -C "$repo" log -1 --format=%s 2>/dev/null)" || return 1
  [ "$head_subj" = "$SUBJ" ] || return 1
  cur_ref="$(git -C "$repo" symbolic-ref --quiet HEAD 2>/dev/null)"
  refs="$(git -C "$repo" for-each-ref --contains HEAD --format='%(refname)' 2>/dev/null)"
  SAW=""
  while IFS= read -r r; do
    [ -z "$r" ] && continue
    [ "$r" = "$cur_ref" ] && continue
    SAW="$r(sha)"
    return 1
  done <<< "$refs"
  if [ "${LEDGER_ID_TEST:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    local tip_tree b b_tree
    tip_tree="$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse "HEAD:.endless/db-ledger" 2>/dev/null)"
    if [ -n "$tip_tree" ]; then
      for b in $(git -C "$repo" for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads/task 2>/dev/null); do
        b_tree="$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse "$b:.endless/db-ledger" 2>/dev/null)"
        if [ "$b_tree" = "$tip_tree" ]; then
          SAW="$b(content)"
          return 1
        fi
      done
    fi
  fi
  return 0
}

record_event() {
  local repo mode payload
  repo="$1"; mode="$2"; payload="$3"
  mkdir -p "$repo/.endless/db-ledger"
  echo "{\"ev\":\"$payload\"}" >> "$repo/$LEDGER"
  git -C "$repo" add "$LEDGER"
  if [ "$mode" = "guard" ] && can_amend "$repo"; then
    git -C "$repo" commit -q --amend --no-edit
    DECISION="AMEND"
  else
    git -C "$repo" commit -q -m "$SUBJ"
    DECISION="APPEND"
  fi
}

REPO=""; WT=""; UP=""
setup() {
  N=$((N+1))
  UP="$ROOT/up$N"
  REPO="$ROOT/repo$N"
  WT="$ROOT/wt$N"
  git init -q --bare "$UP"
  git init -q -b main "$REPO"
  git -C "$REPO" config user.email t@t
  git -C "$REPO" config user.name t
  git -C "$REPO" config commit.gpgsign false
  mkdir -p "$REPO/.endless/db-ledger"
  echo base > "$REPO/src.txt"
  git -C "$REPO" add -A
  git -C "$REPO" commit -q -m "base commit"
  git -C "$REPO" remote add origin "$UP"
  git -C "$REPO" push -q -u origin main
}

upstream_advance() {
  local tmp
  tmp="$ROOT/clone$N"
  git clone -q "$UP" "$tmp"
  git -C "$tmp" config user.email o@o
  git -C "$tmp" config user.name o
  git -C "$tmp" config commit.gpgsign false
  echo upstream >> "$tmp/other.txt"
  git -C "$tmp" add -A
  git -C "$tmp" commit -q -m "upstream: someone else's work"
  git -C "$tmp" push -q origin main
  rm -rf "$tmp"
}

make_task_branch() {
  git -C "$REPO" branch task/900
  git -C "$REPO" worktree add -q "$WT" task/900
  echo "task work" >> "$WT/src.txt"
  git -C "$WT" add -A
  git -C "$WT" commit -q -m "E-900: real user work"
}

try_land() {
  local files
  if git -C "$WT" rebase main >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "OK"
  else
    files="$(git -C "$WT" diff --name-only --diff-filter=U 2>/dev/null | tr '\n' ' ')"
    git -C "$WT" rebase --abort >/dev/null 2>&1
    echo "CONFLICT [${files% }]"
  fi
}

run() {
  local label pull post pre_dec land
  label="$1"; pull="$2"; post="$3"; TAIL="${4:-0}"
  setup

  # ledger events BEFORE the branch exists: no other ref contains HEAD, so the
  # guard permits amend — this is how main's tip becomes an amended commit.
  record_event "$REPO" guard e1
  record_event "$REPO" guard e2

  # Branch forks AT main's ledger tip and stays there — the real shape.
  make_task_branch

  # Probe the guard without mutating anything: expect APPEND (branch is visible).
  if can_amend "$REPO"; then pre_dec="AMEND"; else pre_dec="APPEND"; fi

  upstream_advance
  case "$pull" in
    rebase) git -C "$REPO" -c pull.rebase=true  pull -q --rebase origin main >/dev/null 2>&1 ;;
    merge)  git -C "$REPO" -c pull.rebase=false pull -q --no-rebase --no-edit origin main >/dev/null 2>&1 ;;
    none) : ;;
  esac

  DECISION="-"; SAW=""
  if [ "$post" != "none" ]; then
    record_event "$REPO" "$post" e3
  fi

  # TAIL: further ledger events, always guard-driven, AFTER the post-pull one.
  # Tests whether a single append is enough to re-anchor main permanently.
  local i
  for (( i=0; i<TAIL; i++ )); do
    record_event "$REPO" guard "tail$i"
  done

  land="$(try_land)"
  printf '%-38s | pull=%-6s | post-ledger=%-6s | pre-pull guard=%-6s | post-pull guard=%-6s%s | land=%s\n' \
    "$label" "$pull" "$post" "$pre_dec" "$DECISION" \
    "$([ -n "$SAW" ] && echo " (saw ${SAW##*/})" || echo "")" "$land"
}

run "S1 no pull, ledger (guard)"        none   guard
run "S2 pull --rebase, ledger (guard)"  rebase guard
run "S3 pull --rebase, NO more ledger"  rebase none
run "S4 pull --rebase, FORCED append"   rebase append
run "S5 pull --merge, ledger (guard)"   merge  guard
run "S6 no pull, NO more ledger"        none   none
echo
echo "--- does ONE append after the rewrite re-anchor main permanently? ---"
run "S7 rebase, append once, +5 guard"  rebase append 5
run "S8 rebase, guard only, +5 guard"   rebase guard  5
run "S9 rebase, append once, +20 guard" rebase append 20
```

## From the description

Add a content-level precondition: refuse to amend a ledger tip whose .endless/db-ledger tree any refs/heads/task/* tip holds byte-identically.

keep the existing reachability test alongside it.

fields.title: Show a task's replacement inline with its terminal status
fields.description: Show which task replaced a task inline with its terminal status wherever status appears, and guard against marking shipped work obsolete, which reads as never having happened.
fields.context: `obsolete` reads as "never happened," so there is no way to see at a glance that shipped work was superseded — the fact lives in a `replaced_by` relation that status displays omit, which tempts users to mark shipped tasks obsolete and lose that history.
fields.analysis:
No new status needed.

Three parts: (1) render the relation inline with terminal statuses everywhere status is shown — `assumed (replaced by E-1953)` — in `task show`, `task list` and `session status`; (2) guard `obsolete` on any task that reached unverified/confirmed/assumed/completed, refusing or warning and pointing at `replaced_by` (confirmed absent: setting an `assumed` task to `obsolete` succeeds silently); (3) fix `task update --help`, whose --status list omits `submitted` and `completed` though both are accepted.

fields.title: Replace worktree land's guessed rebase-conflict recoveries
fields.description: Replace the two guessed recovery options in worktree land's rebase-conflict message with guidance that cannot reintroduce identifiers main has deleted and so ship broken code.
fields.context: That happened landing E-1943 against E-1941's deletions.
fields.analysis:
## Note from E-2122 (2026-09-08) — the function this task edits has changed shape

E-2122 ("Report what git actually said when worktree land's rebase fails")
rewrote the surroundings of `_rebase_conflict_message`. Nothing here is
invalidated, but Deliverable 1 now lands on a smaller target than when this plan
was written.

### What changed

Both land call sites (Step 3.7 orphan replay, Step 4 main rebase) previously
caught `CalledProcessError` and called `_rebase_conflict_message`
unconditionally, so every non-zero `git rebase` exit was reported as a content
conflict. They now go through a dispatcher, `_rebase_failure_message`, which
picks one of three reports from evidence rather than from the exit code:

- a rebase that was ALREADY in progress before land started — reported as that,
  left running (land no longer aborts an operation it did not begin)
- unmerged paths present — a real conflict; delegates to
  `_rebase_conflict_message`, unchanged in substance
- anything else — "rebase failed", git's stderr verbatim, and NO recovery
  candidates

Git's stderr is now threaded from the exception into all three; it used to be
captured and discarded.

`_rebase_conflict_message` also had one internal change: the REBASE_HEAD read is
gated on a rebase actually being in progress. REBASE_HEAD is a plain ref, so a
rebase that never started could otherwise report a commit from an unrelated
operation as "your commit that failed to replay".

### What it means for Deliverable 1

Deliverable 1 ("delete the two numbered candidates, end with one instruction:
run `endless worktree diagnose`") still applies, and now applies ONLY to the
conflict branch. The other two branches already offer no candidates — the
non-conflict report deliberately offers none, on the grounds that there is
nothing to judge between once git has named the cause.

So the hazard this task exists to remove — a user following a numbered recovery
that silently reintroduces deleted identifiers — is now reachable through
exactly one path instead of every non-zero rebase exit. The candidates
themselves are untouched and still need deleting.

The auto-file-only confident path is likewise untouched, and this task's
instruction to keep it still holds.

### Cross-reference

E-1347's analysis says the "(none reported)" misclassification "belongs to
E-1957 (and E-1272 for the destructive hint)". The misclassification half is
discharged by E-2122. The destructive-recovery half is still this task's.

E-2122 is pending land at the time of this note; if it has not landed, the
description above is of `task/2122-report-what-git-actually-said-when`.

## From the description

Classification is deterministic even though resolution is not,

so replace guessing with evidence: stop offering candidates, persist the conflict state before the rebase aborts, and add `endless worktree diagnose [E-NNNN]` that classifies (already-landed, auto-file-only, orphaned ledger base, symbol supersession, semantic overlap) and prescribes ONLY what it can prove. Also make `worktree land --dry-run` rehearse the rebase on a throwaway branch — same machinery, and today it cannot preview the failure it exists to preview.

fields.title: Decide how per-worktree sandboxes reach all projects
fields.description: Decide how every project, not only Endless itself, gets a per-worktree sandbox, separating universal per-worktree storage from opt-in routing of database writes to the sandbox.
fields.context:
Sandbox provisioning is gated on `self_dev: true`, so only Endless itself gets per-worktree sandboxes: `_maybe_auto_sandbox_bind` (worktree_cmd.py) returns early for other projects and `config.py` resolves the sandbox root to None for them.

That gate was never an intended design decision — the intent was that EVERY project gets a sandbox, because a sandbox is where a worktree stores the configuration a task needs in order to be verified, and essentially no real software project has zero configuration files.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

State of the code as this task begins, gathered by the E-1941 session on
2026-08-12. Prior knowledge only — conclusions belong in the outcome.

## How the gate is implemented today

- `_maybe_auto_sandbox_bind` (`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`) returns early when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(project_root)` is false, so `task claim` and
  `task spawn` provision a sandbox only for Endless itself.
- `config.py` resolves the sandbox root to `None` for non-self-dev projects
  (`return root if project_is_self_dev(root) else None`).
- `.endless/config.json` carries the flag; only Endless sets it.

A downstream project's worktree therefore gets no sandbox at all — not merely no
sandbox *DB*.

## The two concerns the single flag governs

1. **Per-worktree scratch/config storage.** A worktree needs somewhere to keep
   the configuration a task requires in order to be *verified*. Essentially no
   real software project has zero configuration files, so this is universal.
2. **DB routing.** Endless-specific, and correctly opt-in: a downstream
   project's worktree tasks must land in the real ledger as real audit data, not
   in a throwaway copy. Sandboxing *that* for downstream users would be wrong.

One flag governs both today. Separating them is what this task decides.

## The fault surface is not project-scoped

Relevant because E-1957 (`blocked_by` this task) needs somewhere to persist git
conflict evidence when a land fails, and the existing fault subsystem is the
nearest existing home:

- the `errors` table (`internal/schema/schema.sql`) has no `project_id`
  column — columns are id, code, severity, source, fingerprint, summary,
  occurrences, first_seen_at, last_seen_at, cleared_at, cleared_by
- the JSONL `Detail` struct (`internal/faults/detaillog.go`) has no project
  field
- `monitor.ConfigDir()` (`internal/monitor/db.go`) returns `dbContextDir`
  when set, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/endless`. A land pins `--db main`, which sets
  `dbContextDir` to the real config dir, so the detail log is one shared
  location for every project: `~/.config/endless/log/`

`internal/faults` is otherwise well shaped for this: `Fault.Code` + `Fault.Source`
discriminate the producer, and `Fault.Detail` / `Fault.Fields` carry long
structured capture to the JSONL log by design, explicitly never the DB.

The missing `errors.project_id` is tracked separately as its own defect; it is
not this task's to fix, and this task does not depend on it.

## Adjacent gap, known but out of scope

Neither the `errors` table nor the JSONL detail log has any retention sweep.
`appendDetail` does `MkdirAll` plus append with no rotation; only manual
`endless errors clear` exists. Deliberately left for when it is needed.

## From the description

What is genuinely Endless-specific is only the `endless.db` routing (downstream worktree tasks must still land in the real ledger as real audit data, not a throwaway copy).

So the two concerns are conflated and need separating: per-worktree scratch/config storage should be universal, while sandbox DB routing stays opt-in via self_dev.

fields.title: Decide whether report-minimizer eval data needs a human view
fields.description: Decide whether anyone needs a human-readable view of the evaluation data the report minimizer records, which today can be reviewed only with hand-written SQL.
fields.notes:
Filed as a build task on the assumption a viewer is wanted; the requester has since questioned whether reviewing triples produces any benefit at all, which makes the need the open question rather than the premise.

Partial planning decisions (command shape, render format, no retro-labelling) are recorded there and are contingent on the answer.
fields.context:
E-1953 persists the eval-corpus triple (prompting message, raw draft, minimized output) and its $CUT/$BLOAT/$WRONG/$GOOD label on session_gates, but nothing reads it back for a human — reviewing means hand-written SQL.

Evidence to weigh is in the analysis, including that zero rows have ever carried a label.
fields.analysis:
E-1953 persists the eval-corpus triple (prompting user message, raw draft,
minimized output) plus the `$CUT`/`$BLOAT`/`$WRONG`/`$GOOD` label on
`session_gates`, but nothing reads it back for a human. `task report --raw` is
agent-side and resolves the *calling* session, so from a shell it cannot show
another session's draft. Reviewing the corpus today means hand-written SQL and
a `length()` call to guess whether a cut was reasonable.

That blocks the loop the whole design rests on. The minimizer prompt is
explicitly expected to need substantial tuning, and promotion of an override
into the embedded default is supposed to be gated on beating the current
default OVER THE CORPUS. Neither judging a cut nor running that comparison is
possible without being able to read raw and minimized side by side.

Needed, roughly:

- List recent triples across sessions — when, which session, which task (may be
  null), prompt excerpt, raw/minimized sizes, label. Filterable by label, so
  "show me everything I marked $CUT" is one command.
- Show one triple in full, with raw and minimized presented for comparison
  rather than concatenated. A diff view is the obvious default given the
  minimizer only deletes; a side-by-side is the alternative.
- Read-only, and it must reach the real ledger from a plain shell (the reviewer
  is a human at a terminal, not a session).

Open questions for whoever takes it:

- Command shape. `endless report log` / `endless report show <id>` reads
  naturally but `report` is currently a `task` subcommand, so `endless task
  report --log` may fit the existing tree better at the cost of overloading a
  command that is otherwise agent-facing.
- Whether it also needs an export (JSONL) for running the promotion comparison
  offline, or whether that is a separate concern.

Note for anyone reading the table early: most existing rows predate E-1953 and
carry only `sanctioned_text` — they are E-1901-era relay checkpoints, not
corpus samples. Filtering to rows with a non-null `raw_draft` is what selects
real triples.



---

## Planning session 1 (partial) — decisions and open questions

Planning started in the session that filed this, and stopped early: context was
large, and the requester raised a prior question that should be settled before
any of the below is built. The task was retyped to `brainstorm` at that point,
because the need is no longer the premise — it is the thing to determine.

Everything under "Decided" below is therefore CONDITIONALLY decided: those were
real choices the requester made, but each assumes a viewer gets built at all.
If the prior question resolves the other way they lapse rather than carry
forward, and none of them should be treated as a constraint on the synthesis.

### The prior question, unresolved and load-bearing

**Does reading the corpus actually produce a benefit?** Raised by the requester,
not answered. Everything below assumes it does. Settle this first — if the
answer is no, most of this task evaporates and the remaining need is whatever
the promotion gate strictly requires, which may be a non-interactive export
rather than a viewer.

The case for: judging a cut needs raw and minimized together, and today that is
hand-written SQL. Without it the prompt gets tuned by recollection.

The case against: nobody may actually sit and review triples. The labels the
promotion gate wants arrive live via `$CUT`/`$BLOAT`/`$WRONG`/`$GOOD`, and if
those are the real signal, a viewer is a surface that gets built and not opened.
The honest test is whether the requester would have used it in the last week —
there were ~5 real triples in that span.

### Decided

1. **Command shape — restructure, do not add a sibling group.**
   `task report` becomes a command with subcommands:
   - `endless task report submit --draft-file <path>` — the agent path (what is
     today the bare `task report [<id>] --draft-file`).
   - `endless task report log` — the human review path.

   NOT a new top-level `endless report` group, and not `endless session
   reports`.

   **Consequence the planning session must scope:** this renames the
   agent-facing invocation, which is currently named in SEVEN places, all of
   which must move together or agents will be told to run a command that no
   longer exists:
   - `reportChannelRule` (SessionStart) — internal/hookcmd/claude.go
   - `reportRelayInstruction` (PostToolUse) — internal/hookcmd/claude.go
   - `reportMissingReason` + `relayBlockReason` (Stop bounces) —
     internal/hookcmd/relay_gate.go
   - the spawn handoff close — internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_close.tmpl
   - the respawn handoff — templates/handoff/respawn.md.tmpl
   - the wind-down nudge — src/endless/task_cmd.py
   - docs/guide/tasks.md, index.md, orchestration.md, help/_topics.md
   Plus `tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh` and `e-1973-verify.sh`, which assert the
   current spelling in several places.

   Whether `task report --draft-file` keeps working as a deprecated alias is
   NOT decided. Note that live sessions carry the old spelling in context, so a
   hard break strands every session running at land time.

2. **`show` renders side-by-side columns.** RAW left, MINIMIZED right, aligned.
   Rejected: inline strikethrough (reads as one document but assumes the
   minimizer only deletes), and unified diff (correct under rewording but reads
   as a patch).

   Known cost to solve, not to rediscover: side-by-side wraps badly on tables
   and fenced code blocks — precisely the content the minimizer's invariants
   protect, so it is precisely the content a reviewer is checking. `internal/mdterm`
   already has table rendering that may help.

3. **No retroactive labelling.** The surface stays read-only. Labels keep
   meaning "the user's in-the-moment reaction", which is the more honest signal;
   the cost accepted is that a turn not labelled live can never be labelled.

### Open — do not decide alone

4. **Scope.** Held by the requester for further discussion. The three shapes on
   the table were: read-only viewer; viewer + JSONL export; viewer + export +
   an eval runner that scores prompt A against prompt B over the corpus and so
   implements the promotion gate. This interacts with the prior question above —
   if the viewer is not worth building, the export may still be.

### Facts a planning session should not re-derive

- The triple lives on `session_gates` where `kind_id = 2`: `user_prompt`,
  `raw_draft`, `sanctioned_text` (the minimized output), plus `label` /
  `label_text` and a nullable `task_id`.
- **Most rows are not corpus samples.** As of filing, 60 of 65 rows were
  E-1901-era relay checkpoints carrying only `sanctioned_text`. Filter on
  `raw_draft IS NOT NULL`.
- Zero rows were labelled at that point, which is itself evidence about how much
  signal the live-label path is actually producing.
- Rows persist after `cleared_at` is set, so review reads closed rows; there is
  no retention or pruning policy yet, and the table grows per reported turn.
- `task report --raw` is not a substitute: it resolves the CALLING session, so
  from a human's shell it cannot reach another session's draft.
- This repo ships `"report_gate": false`, so triples accumulate here only from
  voluntary use.

## From the description

Settle that first: if nobody would sit and review, most of this evaporates and what remains is whatever the promotion gate strictly requires — plausibly a non-interactive export, not a viewer.

fields.title: Remove dead sandbox commands and stale binary names

fields.analysis:
# Sandbox tooling rot — inventory

Found while brainstorming E-1958. Mike believed the ephemeral sandbox feature had
been removed from Endless entirely ("we realized YAGNI so we eliminated them from
the Endless feature set") and that `sandbox run`/`enter`/`prune` did not exist.
They do — just not where he looked.

## 1. Error strings name a binary that does not exist

Every error and usage string in `internal/sandboxcmd/` is prefixed
`endless-sandbox <cmd>:` — init.go, bind.go, run.go, prune.go, destroy.go,
list.go. There is no such binary:

```
$ which endless-sandbox
endless-sandbox not found
$ ls cmd/
endless-go
```

The real surface is `endless-go sandbox <cmd>`. `endless sandbox` (the Python
CLI) also does not exist, which is what made the whole feature look absent.
So a user hitting any sandbox error is handed a command they cannot run.

## 2. The ephemeral, non-worktree sandbox path is still live code

`endless-go sandbox --help` lists:

```
  run     [--clone] [--name N] [--keep] -- <cmd> [args]
  enter   [--clone] <name>
  init    [--mode empty|worktree|seed|clone] [--force] <name>
  bind    <worktree-path> [<sandbox-name>]
  list
  prune   [--older-than DURATION]
  destroy [--force] [--if-exists] <name>
```

`run` provisions `modeEphemeral` with a random hex name and auto-destroys on
exit; `enter` forks a subshell; `prune` exists solely to reap orphaned
ephemerals (minimum `--older-than 24h`). None of this is reachable from the
worktree lifecycle, which is 1-to-1 with a task.

Falls out if run/enter/prune go: `modeEphemeral`/`modeKeep`, orphan.go,
supervisor.go, livewriters.go, and the `--clone` flags that only warn about
unimplemented E-1087.

Related: `init --mode seed` and `--mode clone` both hard-exit "not yet
implemented". Dead flags on a live command.

## 3. CLAUDE.md documents the nonexistent binary

The "Self-dev DB sandbox — E-1281" section ends with: "manually
`endless-sandbox destroy e-NNN` if the cache needs reclaiming." Cannot be run.

This item may be moot depending on E-1958: if sandboxes move inside the
worktree they die with it, so manual destroy stops being a thing to document
at all.

## 4. `ENDLESS_SANDBOX` semantics are worth a look while in here

`Sandbox.Env()`  injects `ENDLESS_SANDBOX=<dir>` alongside
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, but only on the run/enter paths — never via `bind`. Its
only consumer is the E-1162 refusal gate in the Python CLI: when set,
project-bound endless subcommands refuse. If run/enter are deleted, nothing
sets the variable and the gate becomes unreachable. Decide whether the gate
goes too, or gets re-keyed onto something that still exists.

## Decision needed

Whether to delete the ephemeral path or keep it deliberately. If deleted, the
`endless-sandbox` → `endless-go sandbox` string fix shrinks to the files that
survive.

## From the description

Decide whether to delete the ephemeral path or keep it deliberately,

then fix the strings in whatever survives.

fields.analysis:
# Renamed identifiers — read this first (2026-08-25)

E-1969 renamed `sessions.active_task_id` to `sessions.task_id` and
`active_epic_id` to `epic_id`. This analysis has been updated to the current
names so a grep for them lands here.

Two things were deliberately NOT rewritten, because they are evidence rather
than description: the quoted `user-machine.jsonl` lines below still read
`old_active_task_id` / `new_active_task_id`, which is what those log entries
literally say (E-1969 renamed the keys for NEW lines only), and the quoted code
blocks are reproduced as the code stood when this was written — E-1968 has since
deleted the reopen-path release entirely.

The open question this analysis ends on — "is the spawn guard keyed on a
now-reliable task_id, on `session_tasks`, or on both?" — was answered on
2026-08-24: `sessions.task_id` alone. See the plan in `--text`.

---

# Evidence

Gathered 2026-08-13 after Mike accidentally spawned a second session on E-1859
instead of resuming the one that had worked it.

## Session→task binding is treated as 1-to-1 in practice, enforced nowhere

Writers create duplicates freely. `task claim` checks the task's status and
resolves a session; it never asks whether another session already holds the
task. `task bind` sets `task_id` with no ownership check at all.

Readers all assume exactly one and silently pick when there is more. Three
places resolve task → session, each ending `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`:

- `monitor.resumeByTask` — `WHERE task_id = ? AND session_id IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY last_activity DESC LIMIT 1`
- `monitor`'s session_focus query — `JOIN sessions bg ON bg.task_id =
  coord.task_id ... LIMIT 1`
- `monitor`'s tmux_lookup query — same shape

So `endless session resume E-NNNN` takes the most recently active session and
gives no signal that it discarded another.

The only place the invariant is named is `release_item`'s refusal when a
different LIVE session owns the task. One guard, on the release path, protecting
an invariant nothing else maintains.

## Why the existing spawn guard did not fire

`task spawn` already refuses when another session owns the task — but the check
is scoped to LIVE sessions. ES-1046 was `ended`, so there was no live owner and
the spawn proceeded.

Keying the guard on `sessions.task_id` would not fix this either: by the
time the spawn ran, that column was already NULL for E-1859 (an earlier
`task reopen` had released it). The only durable record that ES-1046 had ever
worked the task was `session_tasks`.

## Why session_tasks cannot answer "who owned this" today

`session_tasks` has `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id)` and a `relation_id` FK to
`session_task_relations` (1 goal, 2 surfaced, 3 revisited). Per the schema
comment the relation is "set once at capture time by the task-mutation
executors (claim→goal, create/import→surfaced, else→revisited) and never
changed on a later touch."

So a session that first revisits a task and later claims it keeps `revisited`
forever. Observed on E-1859:

    996 → surfaced;  1029, 1043, 1046, 1070 → revisited

ES-1046 held `task_id = 1859` and is nevertheless recorded as
`revisited`. The table can say who saw a task; it cannot say who owned it.

## Mike's design call

Put `relation_id` in the key — `UNIQUE(session_id, task_id, relation_id)` —
rather than making the existing row's relation upgradeable. Upgrading would
overwrite "saw it" with "owned it"; the composite key keeps both, so the history
reads "saw it, then owned it."

This also serves the deliberate fresh-context case: when a task is
intentionally moved to a new session for a clean context, null the old session's
`task_id` and write a `goal` row for the new session. The old session's
`goal` row survives, so "which sessions ever owned E-NNNN" stays answerable.

Open question for implementation: with the relation in the key, does a `goal`
row mean "owned it at some point" or "owns it now"? Append-only ("at some
point") is what recovery needs.



---

# Correction 2026-08-20: what actually NULLs `task_id`

The description previously asserted that `sessions.task_id` "is NULL once
the binding is released" and treated that as a fixed property to design around.
That framing was wrong twice, and it was traced end to end on E-1917.

## Land does not release

E-1917's ledger, in order:

```
task.status_changed  submitted → underway   actor cli 1048
task.claimed                                                 2026-08-07
task.landed          task/1917-…  86b4740                    2026-08-08
task.status_changed  unverified → assumed                    2026-08-08
task.released                                                2026-08-15T06:48:31Z
task.status_changed  assumed → revisit      (same instant)
task.fields_updated  analysis := "# E-1917 post-land defects…"
```

There is no `task.released` at land time. The binding survived the land by a
week. E-1857's machine-local log agrees:

```
2026-08-07T22:39:31Z  reason=claim-event  new_active_task_id=1917
2026-08-15T06:48:31Z  reason=release      old_active_task_id=1917  new=∅
```

## `task reopen` is what released it

The release, the `assumed → revisit` flip and the defect analysis were written in
one burst by one command. `src/endless/task_cmd.py` (the reopen path) does this
before flipping status:

```python
# Clear any lingering session→task binding before flipping status.
# Rare for terminal tasks (worktree land releases), but the plan calls
# for it explicitly so retrospective queries see a clean handoff.
bound_sessions = db.query(
    "SELECT id AS eid FROM sessions WHERE active_task_id = ?", (item_id,))
for s in bound_sessions:
    emit_event(kind="task.released", ..., session_id=str(s["eid"]))
```

and `events.execTaskReleased` runs:

```sql
UPDATE sessions SET active_task_id = NULL, active_epic_id = NULL
 WHERE id = ? AND active_task_id = ?
```

So reopening a task to record defects in its landed work severs the link to the
session that produced that work — in the same command that writes the defect
report. The stated intent is "so retrospective queries see a clean handoff"; the
effect is that retrospection becomes impossible. That is the case to fix.

## Consequence observed

Resuming E-1917 by task ref, and by session ref, both fail.
`ResolveResumeTarget` → `resumeByTask` matches only
`WHERE task_id = ? AND session_id IS NOT NULL`, so with the column NULLed
there is no path from the task back to its claiming session — whose transcript
is intact and whose `task.claimed` event is right there in the ledger. `session
resume` then reports that the session never claimed a task, which is false: it
cannot distinguish *released* from *never claimed*.

## What this changes for this task

Do not key the fix on the assumption that `task_id` goes NULL. Removing
the reopen-path release is part of the work: per ED-1560, `task_id` is
write-once — set at claim, never NULLed and never repointed — and it IS the
ownership record.

That corrects an earlier revision of this note, which said the append-only
`session_tasks` change would supply the durable ownership history. It would not.
`session_tasks` records which tasks a session was INVOLVED with
(goal/surfaced/revisited); involvement is not ownership and cannot stand in for
it. So this task's original premise needs settling before implementation: is the
spawn guard keyed on a now-reliable `task_id`, on `session_tasks`, or on
both? That is a design call, not a detail.

Independent of it, `relation_id` frozen at first touch remains a defect on its
own terms: E-1917's claiming session is still recorded as `surfaced`, stamped when it
filed the task, never upgraded to `goal` when it claimed it.

## Note on actor attribution

Every one of those E-1917 events carries an `actor.session_id` naming the session
being released, while other sessions were doing unrelated work in the same window. For `task.released` that is by construction (`session_id=str(s["eid"])`
names the released session, not the caller). Worth keeping in mind when reading
the ledger for provenance; see also E-1917's own third post-land defect, where
`ENDLESS_SESSION_ID` conflates "route through this session" with "this agent made
the change".

## From the description

The guard needs a durable record of who claimed a task, and `sessions.task_id` is now that record:

That settles the basis this task was waiting on: the guard reads `sessions.task_id`, NOT `session_tasks`, which records INVOLVEMENT (goal/surfaced/revisited) rather than ownership. `session_tasks`' `relation_id` is still written once at first touch and never revised, so a session that files a task and later claims it reads `surfaced` forever — fixed here in the render rather than the schema.

fields.title: Make session movement verbs account for task state
fields.description: Make task reopen, session resume, session goto and task spawn state explicitly what each does to task state and the session's binding, instead of acting on it silently.
fields.context: `task reopen` releases a session's binding silently (its help says 'no session binding', which reads as 'does not create one'). `session resume` clobbers the current pane even when that pane holds live work. `session goto --resume` cannot express intent about a task needing revisit. And `task spawn --reopen` exists only because none of the navigation verbs could change status.
fields.analysis:
# Evidence

Observed 2026-08-13. `endless task reopen E-1859` destroyed ES-1046's
session→task binding without saying so, and neither the user nor the agent that
ran it knew until the loss was investigated hours later.

## What it does

`_reopen_task_core`'s own docstring: "Validates eligibility, releases any
lingering session→task binding, and emits `task.status_changed`."

So the release is intentional. What is not intentional is that it is invisible.
The command printed only:

    Updated E-1859 (Implement the triage job that evaluat...) (text: present):
    • Status: assumed -> revisit

No mention of the released binding. The only record is
`~/.config/endless/log/user-machine.jsonl`:

    ts 2026-08-13T10:05:20Z  session 6b6413b7-...  old_active_task_id 1859
    reason "release"  caller "events.execTaskReleased"

plus a `task.released` event in the ledger.

## The help text says the opposite

`task reopen --help`: "Metadata-only: no worktree creation, no session
binding." That reads as "does not create a binding." It also destroys one.

## Why it matters beyond the surprise

Two consequences, both realised in the incident:

1. `session resume E-NNNN` (the task-keyed form, `monitor.resumeByTask`)
   resolves through `active_task_id`. Clearing it makes the prior session
   unfindable by task. Resume by session id still works, but only if you
   already know the id.

2. Reopen moves the task to `revisit`, which is NOT in
   `_CLAIM_REQUIRES_FORCE`. On `assumed`, `task spawn` refuses with:

       E-NNNN is 'assumed'; pass --reopen to reopen-and-spawn, or run
       `endless task reopen E-NNNN` first.

   `--reopen` inherits the most-applicable prior ended session by default —
   the correct outcome. The other branch that same message offers, running
   `task reopen` first, drops the binding AND moves the status out of the
   guarded set, so a subsequent plain `spawn` proceeds silently. The error
   message routes the user into the trap.

## Mike's design call

Keep the ability to release, but require `--force` for it.

Whatever the gate, the release must be announced — one line naming the session
and task released. A silent destructive side effect on a command documented as
"metadata-only" is the core defect; the flag is the secondary fix.

Consider also whether that error message should stop offering the bare
`task reopen` branch, given where it leads.



---

# 2026-08-20: ED-1560 supersedes §1's design

§1 gates `task reopen`'s release behind `--force` and makes the announcement
unsuppressible. ED-1560 (accepted) removes the operation being gated:
`sessions.active_task_id` is write-once — set at claim, never NULLed and never
repointed. A `--force` flag that permits an unbind is a permission slip for
something the invariant forbids.

Revised shape for §1: `_reopen_task_core` stops emitting `task.released`
entirely. No flag, no announcement, nothing to gate — reopening a task changes
task state and leaves the session binding alone. The misleading help text ("no
session binding") still needs fixing, and the refusal draft in §1 becomes
unnecessary rather than reworded.

## Why this is not theoretical

Traced on E-1917 while diagnosing why its session could not be resumed:

```
task.claimed                                            2026-08-07
task.landed          86b4740                            2026-08-08   ← binding survives
task.released                                           2026-08-15T06:48:31Z
task.status_changed  assumed → revisit   (same instant)
task.fields_updated  analysis := "# E-1917 post-land defects…"
```

One `task reopen` invocation released the binding, flipped the status and wrote
the defect report. Afterwards resuming by task ref and by session ref both fail, and resume
reports that the session never claimed a task —
it reads only the current `active_task_id`, so it cannot tell *released* from
*never claimed*. The session's transcript was intact the whole time; only the
pointer to it was gone. An announcement at reopen time would not have helped: the loss is
discovered a week later, by someone who was not at that terminal.

## Open question for §5 and the `task release` verb — needs Mike

§5 has `task release` move an `underway` task to `revisit`. But `release`'s
defining act is clearing `active_task_id`, which ED-1560 forbids outright. So the
verb's future is a design call, not an implementation detail, and it is not
settled here. Roughly: does `release` become status-only (leaving the binding,
so the session stays reachable), or does it go away, or does ED-1560 carve out an
explicit exception for a user-invoked release? §5 cannot be built until that is
answered.

## Same defect, two more call sites

`monitor.CompleteTask` clears `active_task_id` on completion, and
`monitor.StartChatSession`'s `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET active_task_id=NULL`
clears it for an already-known session id. Both need whatever §1 settles on.
Out of scope: the task-removal clear and the FK's `ON DELETE SET NULL` — the task
itself is gone in those cases.



## Sequencing — E-1969 enforces this with a trigger

E-1969's write-once addendum (added 2026-08-15 from E-1952's session) installs
`sessions_task_id_write_once`, a BEFORE UPDATE trigger that RAISE(ABORT)s on any
change to a non-NULL `task_id` — which covers NULLing as well as re-pointing,
since `NEW.task_id IS NOT OLD.task_id` is true when NEW is NULL.

That makes §1 load-bearing rather than cosmetic. E-1969's own note: "E-1968
(movement verbs) lands with or before this trigger, or every re-pointing verb
starts aborting on contact." `task reopen`'s release is exactly such a verb, so
if §1 still emits `task.released` when the trigger lands, reopen begins failing
at the DB. Removing the emission is therefore the only shape of §1 that works;
`--force` would produce a flag whose success path aborts.

## From the description

Fix together: `--force` plus an unsuppressible announcement on reopen's release; `--force` on resume when the current pane holds a task; `--revisit`/`--no-revisit` on `session goto --resume`; retire `task spawn --reopen`; and rewrite spawn's done-ish refusal, which currently offers 'run task reopen first' as one of two routes — the one that dismantles the guard that produced the message.

fields.description: Rename the session's active task ID column to task ID everywhere it appears, in Go, Python, tests and the session status view, since a session now holds at most one task.
fields.analysis:
# Evidence

Mike's call, 2026-08-13, during the E-1958 session: rename
`sessions.active_task_id` to `sessions.task_id`. Rationale — "active_" was
meaningful when a session might hold several tasks and one of them was the
active one. That is no longer the model: a session holds at most one task, so
the qualifier describes a distinction that no longer exists. Endless has no
external users yet, so there is no reason to carry the legacy name.

## Scope is wider than one column

The name appears across both languages and in a second table:

- Go: the monitor package's session, resume, session_focus, tmux_lookup and db
  paths all name the column in SQL and in struct fields (`ActiveTaskID`);
  `internal/events`'s task-removal executor clears it; `internal/hookcmd`
  reads it.
- Python: session and task command paths read and write it; the pytest suite
  asserts on it directly.
- `session_statuses` carries its own `active_task_id` column with the same
  meaning, and the events executor clears both together. Renaming one without
  the other trades a legacy name for an inconsistent pair.
- `internal/schema/changes/` contains a historical change that recreates the
  sessions table with the old column name. Historical changes must keep
  reproducing the schema as it was at that point — the rename is a NEW change,
  not an edit to an old one.
- `monitor.SessionSnapshot` and `monitor.SessionTxn` both carry
  `ActiveTaskID` / `OldActiveTaskID` / `NewActiveTaskID`, and the latter two are
  serialized into `user-machine.jsonl` as `old_active_task_id` /
  `new_active_task_id`. Renaming the JSON keys breaks readers of existing log
  files; decide explicitly whether the log keeps its current key names.

## Not to be confused with

`sessions.active_epic_id` is a genuinely different thing — the epic a session is
working under while `active_task_id` holds a child. Decide whether it renames
too, or whether "active_" remains correct there because a session's epic and
task are simultaneously active.

## From the description

A session holds at most one task, so the `active_` qualifier names a distinction that no longer exists — it dates from when a session might hold several tasks with one of them active. No external users yet, so there is no reason to keep the legacy name.

Wider than one column: the name appears in the Go monitor SQL and struct fields, the Python session/task paths and tests, and `session_statuses` carries the same column, which should rename with it rather than leaving an inconsistent pair.

Two things to decide explicitly: whether `user-machine.jsonl`'s `old_active_task_id`/`new_active_task_id` keys rename too (breaking readers of existing logs), and whether `sessions.active_epic_id` follows or keeps `active_` since a session's epic and task are simultaneously active.

fields.title: Surface the triager's decision and rationale
fields.description: Surface the triager's recorded decision, rationale and time on task show, so a triaged task can be told apart from one never triaged.
fields.context:
Triage records its call as a task.status_changed event with actor.kind=triager, carrying the deciding model and a one-line rationale in the payload. Nothing reads it. task show displays neither, so a triage decision that lands on unplanned is indistinguishable from a task that was never triaged.

This caused a live misdiagnosis on 2026-08-08: E-1847, E-1891 and E-1893 were manually set to untriaged, the sweep judged all three and routed each back to unplanned with a specific, correct rationale, and the feature was reported as not working because the end state matched the start state.

E-1859's plan called that payload 'what you want when triage starts making calls you disagree with' but never gave it a reader.
fields.analysis: Consider making 'triaged, verdict unplanned' read differently from 'never triaged' wherever untriaged/unplanned are rendered, since that distinction is the whole point of the untriaged status.

fields.title: Fix ledger auto-commit failing on a held git index lock
fields.description: Fix the ledger auto-commit to wait and retry when another writer holds the git index lock, instead of failing with git's raw error and losing the database write.
fields.context: Every event emit runs git add plus git commit --amend on the project's main checkout, because E-1309 routes all ledger commits there — making that one repo a shared write point for every concurrent worktree session, the triage sweep, and any foreground command.
fields.analysis:
## How it was hit

2026-08-08, bulk-routing `unplanned` tasks to `untriaged` from the endless main
checkout, with two other worktree sessions live and the triager on its
15-minute cadence. One `endless task update` carrying 337 ids: 3 applied, the
rest refused with git's raw lock message.

It fails CLOSED — no partial or corrupt state, the DB write simply does not
happen — and chunking into batches of 20 with three retries completed the job.
So severity is friction, not corruption.

## Why it is not just a bulk-operation problem

The contention is between PROCESSES, not within one. E-1309 routes every
session's ledger commits to the single project main checkout, so the writers
are: each concurrent worktree session, the triage sweep, and any foreground
command. Running several parallel worktree sessions is the normal workflow
here, so the collision window exists for a single ordinary write too — it is
just less likely to be observed than in a burst.

Note the monitor's own constant `git worktree list` / `rev-list` polling does
NOT contend: those are reads and take no index lock. The competing writers are
other ledger commits.

## Fix directions

- Retry lock acquisition with backoff in the Go commit path (smallest change).
- Or coalesce appends so one commit covers a burst of events rather than one
  commit per event. The commit already amends into a single `Endless: record
  ledger entry` commit, so the per-event commit is buying nothing that a
  debounced commit would not.

Secondary: the raw git text reaches the user, and the advice it gives — remove
the lock file manually — is wrong for this case and dangerous as a habit.

## From the description

Fix in the Go commit path: retry lock acquisition with backoff, or coalesce appends so one commit covers a burst instead of one commit per event.

fields.title: Gate task report's appeal limit on the report setting
fields.description: Gate task report's one-appeal-per-turn limit on the project's report setting, so projects with the report channel off no longer have a third run refused.
fields.notes: Sibling of E-1966 (the wind-down nudge) and of the PostToolUse fix in E-1953: same class, same principle — off must mean the channel is not there, not that nobody is watching.
fields.context: Reported live by a session in this repo, which ships the gate off.
fields.analysis: The appeal budget is enforcement state — it only means anything when a Stop gate is holding the turn — so where `report_gate` is false it refuses a command nothing is enforcing, on the basis of a counter nothing reads.

fields.title: Fix session liveness duplicating rows for linked tmux panes
fields.description: Fix session liveness to count each tmux pane once when its window is linked into several tmux sessions, instead of multiplying every session's row.
fields.context:
Regression from E-1898, found hours after land.

`tmux list-panes -a` lists a LINKED window's panes once per tmux session the window is linked into (measured:

442 rows for 245 distinct panes, every pane twice).

`list-live` returns 114 rows for 57 sessions and `esu` refuses with 'Multiple sibling Claude panes in this window', blocking worktree entry by session.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

## Symptom

`esu` refuses to resolve with "Multiple sibling Claude panes in this window",
listing the SAME pane twice — identical session id, pane, uuid and worktree.
`session-query list-live` returns 114 rows for 57 sessions. Entering a worktree
by session is blocked.

## Measured

    tmux list-panes -a -F '#{pane_id}' | wc -l        -> 442
    tmux list-panes -a -F '#{pane_id}' | sort -u | wc -l -> 245

Every pane appears exactly twice. `tmux list-panes -a` lists a LINKED window's
panes once per tmux session the window is linked into; nothing in the output
marks the repeat.

## Root cause

`monitor.refreshLiveness` inserts one `live_processes` row per pane returned,
and that TEMP table declares no uniqueness:

    CREATE TEMP TABLE IF NOT EXISTS live_processes (
        kind_id INTEGER NOT NULL, server_uuid TEXT,
        address TEXT NOT NULL, command TEXT)

`session_liveness` LEFT JOINs it on (kind_id, server_uuid, address), so a pane
recorded N times multiplies its session's row N times. Every consumer of the
view inherits the multiplication.

Not the servers: only one socket answers `show-options -gv @server_uuid`, so
`observed_servers` holds one row. The multiplier is purely the pane snapshot.

## Why it was missed

E-1898 states this exact identity for the DURABLE table and explains why the
plain form is insufficient — `processes_identity` indexes
(kind_id, ifnull(server_uuid,''), address) precisely because SQLite treats each
NULL as distinct. The observation table expresses the same identity and does not
enforce it. The reasoning was written down and then not applied one table over.

The tests could not catch it: every fixture seeds `live_processes` through
`SetTestTmuxObservation`, which builds panes from a Go map — inherently unique.
No test ever presented a duplicate address, because no test could.

## Fix

Give `live_processes` the same expression-based unique index as the durable
table, and insert with OR IGNORE:

    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS live_processes_identity
        ON live_processes (kind_id, ifnull(server_uuid,''), address)

A pane seen twice in one snapshot is one pane; the index says so in the same
shape as `processes_identity`, which also covers any future populator (cmux,
herdr) rather than just the tmux path. Deduping in `parsePaneList` alone would
fix today's symptom and leave the invariant unstated.

Apply the same index to `observed_servers` on (kind_id, ifnull(server_uuid,''))
for the same reason — cheap, and removes the sibling failure mode before it
appears.

## Regression test

Seed `live_processes` with the SAME address twice and assert `session_liveness`
still yields exactly one row per session. It must bypass
`SetTestTmuxObservation`'s map (which cannot express a duplicate) and insert
directly, or the test reproduces the blind spot rather than closing it.

## From the description

Fix: give `live_processes` the same expression-based unique index the durable `processes_identity` already uses, insert with OR IGNORE, and do the same for `observed_servers`.

Regression test must INSERT a duplicate address directly — `SetTestTmuxObservation` builds panes from a Go map and cannot express one, which is why no existing test caught this.

fields.title: Build a self-optimizing loop for the report minimizer
fields.description: Build a report minimizer that rewrites and deduplicates against what the user already has, plus an automated optimization loop, scored by a calibrated model judge, that improves it from user labels.
fields.notes: Full design in --analysis; E-1953's viewer-contingent decisions lapse.
fields.analysis:
# Design — the minimizer autoresearch loop

Synthesized in E-1959 (brainstorm). Governing decisions: ED-1555 (free-form
span-scoped labels), ED-1556 (user is a sensor, not a gate), ED-1557 (rewrite
and deduplicate, do not merely delete). Filed as ONE task per ED-1550; grow
children only if it actually stalls.

## What E-1953's planning session decided that now LAPSES

All of it was contingent on a human viewer being built. It is not:

- Side-by-side RAW/MINIMIZED renderer, and the table/code-fence wrapping problem
  it inherited.
- `task report` restructured into `submit` / `log` subcommands, and the
  seven-call-site rename that implied (hookcmd/claude.go, relay_gate.go, the
  handoff templates, task_cmd.py, the guide docs, plus two verify scripts).
- "No retroactive labelling" — still true, but for a different reason: there is
  no review surface to label from.

Do not resurrect any of it. The surviving human-facing surface is one command
(below).

## Objective of the minimizer (ED-1557) — ships as a change

Replaces the shipped `MINIMIZE` prompt in `src/endless/report_prompts.py`:

> Remove things the user can ALREADY see in `session status`; things ALREADY
> written in the task plan or analysis or anywhere else they will have to review
> anyway; replace jargon with clear English; remove or greatly minimize puffery;
> remove anything that is the agent "showing its work."

Deduplication against what the user already has is the novel half, and the half
that forces the fetch policy below.

Delete the deletion-only instruction (l.123-125) and the not-shorter instruction
(l.60).

## Ground truth — two channels, both in the flow of work

1. **Free-form span-scoped labels** (ED-1555), written into the user's ordinary
   replies. `$TOKEN "quoted span"`. Extraction is regex-shaped — something in
   the spirit of `^\$([A-Z]+)` — but **do not lock in that pattern**; it was
   composed ad-hoc as a conceptual example, not as a specification. Synonym
   grouping is the judge's job. Must not fire on a label token legitimately
   quoted inside a reply — same hazard `report_prompts.py` records for the
   denylist.

   **Consistency is leaned on, not enforced.** When a new token clusters near
   one the user has used before, the loop asks in-band whether to merge; the
   user may answer or ignore. Short-term scoring noise from a drifting
   vocabulary is the right trade — a vocabulary the user cannot recall in the
   moment produces NO label at all, and label supply is upstream of everything
   else in the loop. Drift becomes observable rather than silent.
2. **Paired A/B**: on a sampled fraction of turns, produce TWO minimizations and
   let the user pick. This is the only source of a real counterfactual, and it
   is the exact judgment promotion requires ("B beats A"), which an absolute
   label does not supply. Doubling the minimizer call on sampled turns is
   accepted cost.

The A/B sample rate is tuned by asking the user directly, in the reply itself:
each A/B presentation ends by asking whether they want to see these more often
or less often. No config knob — the only seat that can judge the
annoyance-versus-value trade sets it.

### How A/B is presented, and why

The Stop hook compares the **final message** against `task report`'s output, and
a tool call happens BEFORE the final message. So an agent cannot send the A/B
block as its reply and then ask which one won — the reply ends the turn. That
constraint, not aesthetics, picks the shape.

`AskUserQuestion` cannot carry the content either: labels are a few words,
descriptions a sentence. Its `preview` field could hold A and B, but a full
markdown reply rendered in a monospace box reads badly and multi-KB previews are
untested.

**Ship this (option a):** `task report` emits BOTH variants as one sanctioned
output, separated so they are unmistakable —

    ─[Option A of B]────────────────────
    …variant A…
    ─[Option B of B]────────────────────
    …variant B…
    ────────────────────────────────────

— the agent sends that verbatim, and the user picks in their next reply. No gate
change, no new UI, usable immediately.

The pick needs no new parser: `$A` / `$B` is already ED-1555's mechanism, and it
composes — `$B "this sentence"` means "B wins, and that span is still bloat."
Pick and critique in one line.

**Forward-compat worth taking now, cheaply:** make the gate accept ANY OF N
sanctioned texts rather than exactly one. That is the only blocker between
option (a) and both later shapes — `AskUserQuestion` previews with the agent
sending the winner, and a Go/BubbleTea left/right TUI. Explicitly deferred: the
TUI is a later enhancement, not part of getting something usable.

**The doubling.** On sampled turns the user reads the loser too. The minimizer
exists to cut what they read, and A/B doubles it. Two separate things follow —
one about measurement, one about display.

**Measurement: exempt A/B turns from length analysis.** Score each variant on
its own length; never count the doubled total against the minimizer. The
doubling is the cost of the experiment, not a failure of the prompt. Fair
because it is opt-out: a user who tunes the minimizer to their satisfaction
turns the optimizer off and never sees a pair again.

**Do NOT instead instruct the minimizer to aim shorter on A/B turns.** That is a
different lever and it poisons the result: both variants would be produced under
a length constraint production never applies, so the comparison would say which
prompt wins AT HALF LENGTH — promoting a winner never tested under the
conditions it will actually run in.

**Display: preview, then read in full on demand.** Show the first few lines of
each variant inline, and let the user open either in full, with color, via
`endless session turn A|B -p`. This reuses the command already being built
rather than inventing a terminal diff layout, and it needs no special case for
the hard scenario (A and B diverging broadly).

Considered and rejected: rendering the shared text once and duplicating only
divergent spans. Correct in principle, but substantial effort and hard to make
graspable in a terminal.

Consequence for the read command: `session turn` must address variants of the
PENDING turn, not only past turns — `A`/`B` join the offset as arguments.

## The judge

Scores every turn, labelled or not, from `(user_prompt, raw, minimized,
fetched_context)`. Dense and unlimited — the only thing that can evaluate a
variant over the whole corpus.

Human labels do NOT score prompts; they **calibrate the judge**. The judge
commits to a prediction BEFORE seeing the user's reaction (which of A/B they
will pick; whether they will flag the turn). Rolling prediction-vs-outcome
agreement is the health number. Per ED-1556, low agreement raises the A/B
sample rate and is announced in-band; it never halts promotion silently.

## Scoring — vetoes, not a weighted sum

1. **Mechanical invariants** — no model call. Fenced code blocks and tables
   survive byte-for-byte; a command the user must run survives. NOTE: the
   subsequence check (minimized ⊆ raw) **dies with deletion-only** — rewriting
   is the objective now, so only the byte-exact protected-content checks remain
   mechanical.
2. **Fidelity** — the judge.
3. **Compression** — free, saturating.

A variant buying compression at the cost of one invariant violation is not
better; a weighted average would make that trade. Vetoes, then maximize
compression subject to no fidelity regression.

Adding a self-scored compression target to the prompt is a legitimate variant
precisely BECAUSE invariants are enforced separately.

**Rejected as a score component: label count / label rate.** It measures the
user's engagement, not the prompt — turning the gate on will raise it while
quality is unchanged. Instrumentation health metric only.

## Monitoring vs. deciding — do not conflate

- **Monitoring**: rolling metrics over live traffic. "Are we drifting?"
  Confounded by corpus drift. Alarm, not verdict.
- **Deciding**: paired replay of variants over a FROZEN corpus; item difficulty
  cancels. The only thing that may gate a promotion.

## Search space — three axes, jointly, per task type

Variants are **generated by the optimizer**, not hand-written by an agent.
Seeded from known compression grammars and free to diverge: ASD-STE100, Attempto
Controlled English (ACE), Plain English Foundation Standards, CNL-P, RICECO/ICC,
PDL. Plus orthogonal style axes (all-bullets vs. prose).

1. **Prompt text**
2. **Fetch policy** (below)
3. **Bypass threshold** — length under which a reply skips the minimizer
   entirely. Latency and cost are a big factor. 256 was a guess; the shortest
   draft in the corpus is 396 chars and ZERO of 23 passed through untouched, so
   there is no evidence yet about behavior below any threshold.

**Split by task type NOW**, not later — variants keyed `(task_type, hash)`.
Coordinating a follow-up task later costs the user more than splitting up front.
Sample volume is not a constraint worth designing around.

## Fetch policy — and why the corpus row must grow

The dedup objective cannot be scored from the triple alone. Two proposals turned
out to be one mechanism:

- The minimizer **fetches** what it wants (`task show E-nnnn --text`, session
  status, sibling tasks, …), and
- the corpus row **records what was requested and what came back**.

A tool-using minimizer is nondeterministic in its INPUTS, which breaks replay:
A/B over a frozen corpus is meaningless if each run re-fetches live state that
has since changed. Replay must serve context from the record, never re-fetch.
So fetching forces recording; they are the same mechanism.

The set of things it MAY fetch is large and declared. **What it actually fetches
is a JSON policy document the optimizer maintains** — the third tunable axis.
"Give it everything every turn" fails on cost and latency, not principle, which
is exactly what makes the policy worth optimizing rather than fixing.

**Not backfillable.** Rows written before this exists can never gain the context.

## The one surviving human surface

A command that dumps the RAW draft for a turn, verbatim — **no diff, no
columns**. The user keeps the minimized text in an adjacent tmux pane and
compares by eye. This replaces E-1953's side-by-side renderer entirely.

Shape:

    session turn [<offset>] [-p]

- **0-based, counting back, no negative sign.** `session turn` = `session turn
  0` = most recent. If the latest turn is #503, `session turn 3` is #500.

  Considered and rejected: a negative offset (`session turn -2`). Same mental
  model — "now minus N" — but a leading `-` collides with flag parsing, forcing
  `--` or special-casing, which is boilerplate on every invocation. The
  direction is already implied by "back", so the sign carries nothing.

  **The help text is what makes 0-based read naturally: say "N turns back", not
  "the Nth turn."** Under the second wording 0-based is surprising; under the
  first it is obvious. This was very nearly mis-designed as 1-based on the
  strength of bad phrasing alone.

- `A` / `B` are also valid arguments, selecting a variant of the pending turn
  (see the A/B display note above).
- `-p` paginates, matching `task show -p`.
- Deliberately NOT under `task report`, which is agent-facing.

Two things it needs that are easy to miss:

- **A session selector.** The reviewer is reading a PANE's session, not their
  own. Default to the session bound to the current tmux pane, with an explicit
  `ES-nnnn` override.
- **Real-ledger access from a plain shell.** `task report --raw` does not
  qualify: it resolves the CALLING session and so can never reach another
  session's draft.

## Storage and versioning

- **Corpus stays in the ledger DB.** The concern was duplicated copies of the
  same text, not the table. Versioned history of discussions is wanted. Revisit
  if secrets leaking into a version-controlled ledger becomes the operative
  worry — that, not bloat, would be the reason to move it.
- **No embedded git repo for prompt versioning.** Content-address variants:
  `(hash, text, parent_hash, created_at, note)`. Every eval run must reference
  its variant inside the store regardless, so adding git creates two identities
  for one object plus a sync problem. `parent_hash` gives lineage — the only
  thing git supplied. Diff at read time. Rollback of a bad auto-promotion is a
  pointer move, which is what makes removing the approval step safe.

## Config

- `report_gate` → **`minimizer`**, as an object:
  `{"enabled": true, "optimizer": true}`. Old name is cryptic inside-baseball;
  the object admits the second switch. Needs a fallback read for the old key.
- Set `enabled: true` in this repo as part of this work. The original exemption
  (a session tuning the prompt should not be governed by the prompt it edits)
  weakens once tuning is automated.

## Scheduling

Rides the **existing fire-once job runner**. A dedicated scheduler is a later
question, if ever.

## Corpus state at design time

23 real triples (`raw_draft IS NOT NULL`) of 83 rows; the rest are E-1901-era
relay checkpoints carrying only `sanctioned_text`. Zero labelled — expected,
since the gate is off here. Keep-ratio by draft size: 256-512 → 0.81,
512-1k → 0.67, 1k-2k → 0.62, 2k+ → 0.86. The 2k+ figure is the defect ED-1557
fixes.

## The earliest observable that the loop is learning

This is NOT an experiment to specify and run. The loop is a continuous learning
process, not a numbered series someone designs in advance — nothing here should
be read as "define experiment 1, then experiment 2."

It is simply the first thing that will become visible: keep-ratio by draft-size
bucket, re-measured as the rewriting objective takes hold. The 2k+ bucket
drifting down from 0.86 toward the 0.62 of smaller drafts is the cheapest early
sign the loop is doing something. Watch it; do not steer by it.

## From the description

The user supplies ground truth in the flow of work via free-form span-scoped labels (ED-1555) and picks between paired A/B minimizations; an LLM judge scores every turn and is calibrated by blind prediction against those reactions. The optimizer generates variants — seeded from controlled-English grammars — and jointly tunes prompt text, a JSON fetch policy, and the bypass threshold, split by task type. Promotion is decided by paired replay over a frozen corpus with invariant vetoes, never by a weighted average or a rolling mean. Rides the existing job runner.

fields.title: Add project status and project monitor
fields.description: Add project status and project monitor, project-wide counterparts of the session pair that triage attention across many concurrent sessions, putting unverified tasks and waiting sessions first.
fields.notes: Per E-1815.
fields.context: Its job is attention triage across many concurrent sessions — unverified tasks sort to the top, and sessions paused on a permission prompt read as loud "waiting on you".
fields.analysis:
Today "needs attention" is signalled only by red color and an asterisk on tmux
window tabs, which does not scale to ~70 concurrent sessions (all one project at
present). This display is the answer to managing that.

Unverified sorts first because unverified work is what accumulates unseen — 57
unverified tasks in `endless` (75 machine-wide, 71 of them 30-90 days old)
accumulated precisely because there was no way to keep it in view, worsened by
two tmux crashes that took it out of sight.

Stalled sessions: auto-spawn's cap (E-1814) deliberately counts a session paused
on a permission prompt against itself, on the reasoning that a prompt is a claim
on the user's attention and the cap measures claims on attention. That is only
safe if this display makes the stall loud. This is therefore load-bearing for
auto-spawn, not polish.

tmux topology: its own tmux session, two panes — the monitor, plus a bare shell
for running `endless` commands against what it shows. (The bare shell is
agentenv `unknown`; the CLI fails open and the hook no-ops there, which is the
desired behavior.) Auto-spawned session windows deliberately do NOT land here —
they land interleaved in the user's own tmux session (E-1814), because a
separate review-batch session is out of sight, out of mind, which is the exact
failure mode that produced the unverified sediment.

Auto-spawn on/off: this window fires the E-698 fire-once runner, so auto-spawn
(E-1812/E-1814) runs only while it is open. Closing it is a zero-code kill
switch. Deliberate for v1 — surviving a closed window is the point at which a
daemon is being chosen, and that should be a later explicit decision.

Out of scope, named in E-1815 and not filed: collapsible tree view, jumping to a
session in another terminal from this window, auto-verify/auto-land, stall
detection.

## From the description

`project status` is the static render, `project monitor` the live one, same relation as the existing session pair.

One piece of work, not two.

Runs in its own dedicated two-pane tmux session and is what fires the E-698 runner, making it the on/off switch for auto-spawn.

fields.description: Decide the mechanism for draining the unverified task backlog, such as a script, a command, a background job or an agent pre-classification pass, as each task needs its own judgment.
fields.notes: Per E-1815.
fields.context:
57 tasks in endless (75 machine-wide, 71 of them 30-90 days old).

Each needs per-task judgment: still current, superseded, obsolete, or confirmable.

Catch a fish versus build a fish-catching machine.
fields.analysis:
Surfaced in E-1815 while designing auto-spawn's backpressure cap. The cap was
originally going to count total unverified tasks; measurement showed 57 in
`endless` / 75 machine-wide with 71 of the 75 aged 30-90 days, which is sediment
rather than a queue and would have made the cap unclearable. Auto-spawn's cap
was rescoped to count only auto-spawned unverified, so this backlog no longer
blocks that feature — the two are orthogonal.

Highest-leverage item surfaced in that conversation by ED-1550's own arithmetic:
closing is named there as the only fast lever on the file-to-close ratio, and
most of these probably shipped months ago and simply never got confirmed.

Why the sediment exists (diagnosed in E-1815): it accumulated before the session
monitor existed, when there was no good way to keep track of unverified work,
and two tmux crashes took unverified tasks out of sight.

That diagnosis narrows this task. The PREVENTION half is already in flight — the
session monitor exists, and E-1976 (project monitor) surfaces unverified first by
construction, so new sediment should stop forming. What is unbuilt is the DRAIN.
Scoped here to draining; widen it if that turns out wrong.

Existing coverage checked before filing: E-1881 (continuous auto-merge job for
endless-managed worktree commits) and E-1882 (`worktree reconcile` for stale
endless-managed commits) cover GIT currency — whether a worktree's commits can be
brought current. Neither covers TASK-STATUS currency, which is what this is.
Whatever mechanism this brainstorm lands on should check whether it can lean on
those two for the git-side signal rather than re-deriving it.

## From the description

The question is the mechanism, not the verdicts: ad-hoc script, a new CLI verb, a background job, an agent pass that pre-classifies for human ratification, or something else.
